item.title: How Composition and Cluster Structure Influence CO Adsorption in Pt and Pt–Ge Clusters
item.description: Ge incorporation can weaken CO adsorption on Pt clusters, but it also changes their geometry and bonding. We combine density functional theory with advanced chemical bonding analysis to examine the interplay between composition, geometry, electronic structure, and CO adsorption in ten-atom Pt10, Pt6Ge4, Pt5Ge5, and Pt4Ge6 clusters. By generating derivative structures through Pt/Ge substitution in previously reported global-minimum geometries, we examine how composition and starting structure affect CO binding. For the two pure Pt isomers, we also compare CO binding at the same spin multiplicity. Chemical bonding analysis reveals a transition from predominantly delocalized multicenter bonding in pure Pt clusters to more localized covalent bonding in PtGe clusters. Effective coordination numbers, PtC bond lengths, and bond critical point electron densities are then used to characterize the local environment and bonding of adsorbed CO. However, these descriptors do not consistently correlate with CO binding energies. Energy decomposition reveals that adsorption strength reflects a composition-and site-dependent balance between the frozen-fragment cluster–CO interaction and metal-cluster reorganization. Remarkably, structural reorganization can even reverse the binding-energy trend predicted from the interaction energy alone. These findings demonstrate that CO binding energy, which depends on both the adsorbed complex and the chosen bare-cluster reference, does not necessarily reflect the intrinsic strength of the PtCO interaction. We therefore highlight the importance of combining adsorption energies with local bonding descriptors and fragment-energy analysis to disentangle electronic and structural contributions to CO affinity in these ten-atom clusters.

item.title: Microstructure-resolved modeling of fused filament fabrication of lithium-ion battery electrodes
item.description: Lithium-ion battery (LIB) electrode microstructure can be flexibly tailored via solvent-free extrusion followed by fused filament fabrication (FFF) printing. However, the influence of extrusion and printing process parameters on the final electrode microstructure, properties, and electrochemical performance remains insufficiently explored and has never been investigated through computational modeling. Herein, we introduce a sequential, particle-resolved framework that transfers heterogeneous filaments from our previously developed twin-screw extrusion model into FFF simulations. The FFF model incorporates solid granules and a viscous fluid, representing active materials and binder/conductive phases, with a material cooling law. Single-strand deposition, one- and two-layer printing simulations, used here as a proof of concept, examine filament feed velocity, printing speed, nozzle-bed gap, cooling rate, strand spacing distance, and interlayer arrangement. Geometrical characterization and through-thickness transport analyses quantify void fraction, tortuosity factors, apparent electronic conductivity, and whole-structure electronic resistance of the final two-layer electrodes. Strand spacing strongly affects layer coverage, surface height uniformity, and inter-strand overlap. Two-layer microstructures with similar total void fractions and tortuosity factors exhibit nearly twofold differences in apparent electronic conductivity. This framework lays the foundation for studying the relationships between microstructure and performance in solvent-free LIB electrode manufacturing via extrusion and 3D printing.

item.title: Predicting nanosurface properties via Rayleigh instability
item.description: The surface tension, γ , of nanoscale clusters deviates from its planar limit, γ∞, based on the value of the Tolman length, δ , which is difficult to compute. In this study, we introduce a new method that exploits the Rayleigh instability of charged nanosurfaces to compute both γ∞ and δ properties. By combining Tolman’s γ formulation with the Rayleigh limit we compute these properties only based on the cluster size and charge under which the instability is triggered. We validate the method via molecular dynamics simulations of five SPC/E water nanoclusters with solvated electrons and radii of 2-4 nm. We find γ∞ = 58.29±1.11 mN/m, which agrees within 1.2 standard deviations of the planar slab simulation, and δ = −0.45± 0.29 Å, which agrees with literature estimates for SPC/E water. The method requires only standard simulations and a simple fitting, and is expected to be applicable to experimental measurements of the Rayleigh limit.

item.title: Stable Pt Single Atoms Embedded in Ge(001) Enable Efficient Hydrogen Evolution
item.description: Single-atom catalysts offer a promising route to maximize noble-metal utilization, but maintaining isolated active sites under operating conditions remains a major challenge. Pt deposition on Ge(001) induces the spontaneous formation of thermodynamically stable nanowire arrays in which Pt atoms remain atomically dispersed within the Ge lattice, creating well-defined single-atom catalytic sites. Here, we investigate the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) on Pt–Ge(001) using grand-canonical density functional theory under constant-potential conditions, explicitly accounting for the effects of electrode potential, hydrogen coverage, solvent effects, and pH. Hydrogen adsorbs selectively on Pt sites, while the Ge environment stabilizes the Pt atoms and tunes their hydrogen-binding properties. The calculated activation barriers favor a Volmer–Heyrovsky pathway, with facile Volmer adsorption promoting hydrogen accumulation under cathodic conditions. At 1 ML hydrogen coverage, the calculated Volmer and Heyrovsky barriers are substantially lower than reported values for Pt(111), indicating competitive HER kinetics. These results identify Pt–Ge(001) nanowire arrays as a promising platform for the HER and demonstrate how the interplay between support-induced stabilization, electrode potential, and adsorbate coverage can govern the activity and reaction mechanism of single-atom electrocatalysts.

item.title: PanJAK: predicting selectivity across the JAK family with deep learning
item.description: Predicting selectivity between closely related protein targets remains a major challenge in drug discovery. While drug-target affinity (DTA) models typically focus on predicting activity against individual targets, selectivity depends on resolving differences in activity between them. Here, we introduce panJAK, a DTA framework to predict selectivity across the four Janus kinase (JAK) paralogs. The model combines molecular representations with a ligand-conditioned encoding of structurally aligned binding pockets and predicts cross-paralog selectivity from differences in potency without requiring a selectivity-specific training objective. Using a curated dataset of approximately 10,000 compounds, we demonstrate that panJAK improves the quantitative prediction of selectivitywindows compared to established baseline models under scaffold-disjoint evaluation. Errors in individual potency predictions were positively correlated across paralogs and partly cancelled upon subtraction, resulting in more accurate selectivity estimates than expected under independent errors. Although prediction errors increased with chemical novelty, calibrated prediction intervals allowed for the identification of a subset of comparisons with high retrospective directional accuracy. These findings highlight the potential of adapting affinity-prediction models to address quantitative selectivity across homologous targets, supporting compound prioritization based on predicted selectivity profiles and associated reliability of those predictions.

item.title: Beyond Storage Modulus: Toward Application-Relevant Rheological Assessment of Dynamic Hydrogels
item.description: Hydrogels designed for injection and extrusion-based bioprinting experience a sequence of mechanical environments that a single small-amplitude storage-modulus value cannot capture. Before processing, a formulation may need to remain homogeneous and resist premature flow; during delivery, it must deform under device-imposed stresses without excessive pressure or payload damage; after deposition, it must recover sufficiently to retain its intended geometry; and during subsequent use, it must respond appropriately to sustained loading, fluid exchange, degradation, and cell-generated forces. This critical narrative review examines the rheological measurements needed to characterize these distinct stages. This review considers linear viscoelasticity, flow curves, operational yielding, large-amplitude oscillatory shear, stress relaxation, creep, and post-shear recovery alongside direct injection and printing outcomes. Primary studies show that rapid restoration of elastic dominance does not equal complete restoration of the original modulus; that printability depends on the ink, support bath, nozzle, and process settings as a coupled system; and that matrices with similar initial stiffness can produce different cellular responses when their relaxation kinetics differ. More recent work also highlights trade-offs between rapid stress relaxation and long-term mechanical stability, and links extrusion-induced stress and residence time to cell viability. We discuss methodological concerns, including wall slip, sample history, geometry effects, and the mismatch between rotational rheometry and nozzle flow. We propose an application-led assessment framework and a minimum reporting checklist that connect each performance claim to a corresponding experiment. The central argument is that rheological characterization should progress from reporting isolated material descriptors toward testing whether those descriptors explain or predict application-specific performance.

item.title: Multidisciplinary Design and Characterization of Novel cis- and trans-Ferrocene–Platinum Anticancer Candidates
item.description: The limitations of the classical platinum-based drugs (i.e. cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin), such as adverse side-effects and drug resistance, highlight the need to develop alternative metal-based anticancer compounds. In this context, molecules that bear two pharmacologically active motifs represent a versatile strategy, as they may enhance therapeutic efficacy through synergistic effects, being the synthesis of this type of drugs a promising research field. In the present study, we report the preparation and characterization of new heterometallic Pt(II) complexes bearing the p-ferrocenylaniline ligand (L) using K2[PtCl4] and cis-[PtCl2(DMSO)2] as precursors. The reactions lead to mixtures of the cis and trans isomers of the products [PtCl2L2] and [PtCl2(DMSO)L], isolating only one isomer in both cases: the cis isomer for the disubstituted complex and the trans for the monosubstituted product. Different synthetic routes are explored to assess the influence of solvent polarity, reaction time and temperature on the formation of the cis/trans isomers of [PtCl2(DMSO)L]. The results are supported by the thermodynamic stability obtained by DFT calculations, considering none or four explicit solvent molecules of water, acetone or dichloromethane, observing an increase in the Boltzmann distribution of the cis isomer with the solvent polarity. A more in depth study of the non-covalent interactions between the isomers and the solvent molecules is performed. Alternatively, the study of the reaction mechanism to afford the isomers of [PtCl2(DMSO)L] suggests an isomerization process from the cis to the trans isomer through a dissociative pathway, which is enhanced due to the presence of the aromatic moiety in the ferrocene ligand. These findings offer new insight into controlled isomer formation in ferrocene-containing Pt(II) complexes and may contribute to the rational design of heterometallic anticancer agents.

item.title: Light-Driven Active Transport across a Liquid Membrane via Photoswitch Sensitization
item.description: Active transport across membranes is essential in living systems, but its implementation in artificial systems remains challenging. Light-driven active transport based on photoswitchable carriers requires differential illumination on the opposite sides of the membrane, a constraint that prevents its application to nanoscale membranes. Here, we introduce a photosensitization-based strategy that enables active transport across a liquid membrane using a single light source. By confining a ruthenium sensitizer in one aqueous compartment, single light irradiation generates different photostationary states of a cationic azobenzene carrier on the two sides of the membrane. The resulting difference in carrier permeability drives the transport of the carrier, together with its counterion, against a concentration gradient. These results establish photosensitization as a means to achieve light-driven active transport under uniform irradiation and provide a basis for its implementation in bilayer membranes.

item.title: Forced Degradation of Bromantane: Preliminary Characterization of an Oxidative Degradation Product Using Liquid Chromatography and High-Resolution Mass Spectrometry
item.description: Bromantane (N-(4-bromophenyl)adamantan-2-amine) is a synthetic adamantane derivative developed as an antiasthenic pharmaceutical agent in Russia. Despite its pharmaceutical applications and relevance to anti-doping analysis, the chemical degradation pathways of bromantane remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigated the forced-degradation behavior of bromantane under acidic, alkaline, thermal, and oxidative conditions using liquid chromatography with ultraviolet detection (LC-UV) and Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). Bromantane remained the predominant chromatographic component following acidic, alkaline, and thermal exposure. In contrast, oxidative exposure resulted in the disappearance of the distinct bromantane UV peak and the appearance of a new chromatographic peak at 20.43 and 20.48 min in two independent preparations. Mass spectrometric analysis revealed a characteristic bromine isotope doublet at nominal m/z 320 and 322. Following retrospective correction of a systematic mass offset, the observed masses were consistent with a proposed neutral molecular formula of C16H18BrNO, corresponding to the addition of one oxygen atom and the loss of two hydrogen atoms relative to bromantane. A nitrone derivative is proposed as a potential structural candidate, although alternative structural isomers cannot be excluded without additional spectroscopic characterization. Substantial variability in integrated peak areas prevented reliable quantification of degradation. These findings provide preliminary insight into the oxidative susceptibility of bromantane and a basis for further degradation-product characterization and analytical method development; no prior forced-degradation study of bromantane was found in the databases searched.

item.title: Optical Polymer Structure Recognition with PolymerScribe and an Iterative Train-Predict-Correct Workflow
item.description: Immensely valuable polymer information remains functionally inaccessible, trapped in the chemical structure images of legacy and contemporary publications. However, without labels such as molblocks or string representations, those images are not directly processible by cheminformatic tools for downstream applications. This work develops an image recognition model, PolymerScribe, and demonstrates an iterative train-predict-correct workflow for curating labeled polymer structures from the literature. Building on top of previous work for molecular image recognition, PolymerScribe was trained to recover both the molecular graph and the S-group information including bracket locations, superscripts, and subscripts, allowing for subsequent conversion to BigSMILES line notation. After bootstrapping PolymerScribe with a small labeled subset consisting of 300 pairs of images and molblocks, the model was iteratively improved using selected batches of unlabeled polymer images. In each iteration, PolymerScribe predicted molblock labels which were then manually corrected, and the model was retrained with the newly labeled images. This iterative process ultimately led to PolymerLit, the first benchmark dataset for Optical Polymer Structure Recognition (OPSR), consisting of more than 1,700 polymer images from open access journal articles with corresponding molblocks that have been manually verified and corrected, along with canonical BigSMILES representations. Even when trained on a small dataset of labeled images, PolymerScribe correctly predicted the canonical BigSMILES for 58% of unseen structures (90% for molecules with fewer than 20 heavy atoms) in retrospective testing. PolymerScribe and PolymerLit are freely shared with the community as a starting point towards larger-scale information extraction from polymer literature.

item.title: A Computational Protocol for Accurate Pressure-Dependent Rates in Barrierless Addition Reactions: CN and C2H Reactivity with Ethylene
item.description: The accurate determination of rate coefficients and product branching fractions for multi-well reactions with barrierless entrance and/or exit channels remains a major challenge in computational kinetics, particularly when widely different temperature and pressure regimes must be considered. Here, we introduce a general computational protocol for the case of addition reactions that integrates accurate yet affordable electronic-structure calculations with statistical kinetic treatments tailored to the different elementary reaction steps and a multi-well master-equation approach. The reactions of the CN and C2H radicals with ethylene are selected as representative test cases to assess the accuracy and reliability of the proposed methodology. The reactive potential energy surface (PES) is characterized using revDSD-PBEP86-D3(BJ) geometries and junChS energies. While barrierless entrance channels are treated using variable reaction coordinate transition state theory, competing hydrogen-abstraction pathways are described through variational transition state theory, and unimolecular transformations through conventional transition state theory. Comparison with HEAT-like reference energy calculations, performed on top of CCSD(T)-F12 optimized geometries, demonstrates that the working electronic-structure protocol reproduces relative energies with mean unsigned deviations of 1.9 and 2.5 kJ mol−1 for C2H and CN, respectively. The predicted total rate coefficients agree with available experimental measurements generally within a factor of 1.5. More importantly, the results establish a hierarchy of accuracy requirements: the entrance-channel interaction potential and its variational treatment primarily control the overall addition rate coefficients, whereas accurate PES energetics and collisional energy-transfer parameters are essential for predicting product branching fractions. For competing hydrogen-abstraction reactions, accurate barrier heights and variational corrections become particularly important at elevated temperatures. These findings provide a general framework for the reliable and computationally efficient investigation of barrierless addition reactions, identifying the key methodological ingredients required to predict their kinetics across different physical environments.

item.title: Boronium-Based Ionic Liquids: From an Unusual Main-Group Cation to Functional Ionic Materials
item.description: Boronium-based ionic liquids, sometimes referred to by the acronym “BILs”—are salts in which the cation is a tetra-coordinate, boron-centred molecular ion, and which occupy a distinctive intersection of main-group, coordination and ionic liquid chemistry. Their modern development largely began with robust L1L2BH2+ ions (L = Lewis-base ligand) and the recognition that appropriate ligand and anion choices can render these salts room-temperature liquids. Two decades of work now support a coherent materials picture involving them: nitrogen-donor boronium cations can combine low glass-transition or melting temperatures with useful ionic conductivity, wide electrochemical stability windows and exceptional resistance to reduction at lithium metal. These attributes have led to the creation of durable lithium-metal cells, high-voltage electrochemical double-layer capacitors, and polymerizable electrolyte platforms. Pairings with certain anions have yielded low-viscosity hypergolic fuels; deliberately lipophilic/amphiphilic structures have served as ashless lubricant additives, and can display antibacterial, antifungal and antiviral activity. Their structural variety has simultaneously expanded beyond canonical N,N-donor frameworks to cations in which ureas and amides serve as O-donor ligands, and to hydrolytically robust salts of +3 boronium ions. This review maps out chemically rigorous bounds for BILs, reconciles nomenclature and electronic-structure descriptions, surveys synthesis and property relationships, benchmarks the best-supported applications, and identifies places where data remains sparse. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing formal charge bookkeeping from the distributed charge of real cations, on avoiding an unsupported general description of B–H bonds as hydridic, and on separating useful screening metrics from device-level validation. The emerging design paradigm for these salts is not simply “put boron somewhere in an ionic liquid”; rather, it is to co-design donor set, cation shape, anion chemistry, interfacial reactivity and phase behaviour as one coupled system.

item.title: A Rigid Diene, Two Electron Counts: 16– and 18–Electron Ni(0) Olefin Complexes
item.description: We report the application of a rigid polycyclic cage–diene (PCCD) as a ligand for Ni(0) complexation. Microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED) of Ni(PCCD)2 revealed a mixture of isomers: 16-electron Ni(η4–PCCD)(η2–PCCD) and 18-electron Ni(η4–PCCD)2 complexes. Compared to commercially available Ni(0) sources, Ni(PCCD)2 exhibited comparable catalytic activity in Buchwald–Hartwig aminations.

item.title: Ligand-Coupled Electron Transfer Enables Highly Stable Two-Electron Electrochemical Energy Storage using a Nickel Bis(diphosphine) Complex
item.description: Here, we show that highly stable two-electron (2e−) energy storage is achieved using [NiII(dppe)2](BF4)2 (dppe = 1,2-bis(diphenylphosphino)ethane) in combination with chloride and bromide salts and excess dppe ligand. Halide coordination to [NiII(dppe)2] 2+ is shown to yield mono-halide [NiII(dppe)2X]+ and bis-halide NiII(dppe)X2 complexes in equilibrium (KCl = 1.4 and KBr = 0.015), both of which are reduced by 2e− to yield Ni0(dppe)2. Controlled addition of halide and excess dppe ligand shifts the equilibrium toward [NiII(dppe)2X]+ and compresses the 1e− redox events to less than 100 mV, resulting in effective 2e− storage at the same potential (−0.89 V (Cl−) and −0.85 V vs Fc+/0 (Br−)). Cyclic charge-discharge experiments in three-electrode H-cells at the optimized halide/dppe conditions yield highly stable 2e− redox cycling with exceptionally low capacity fade rates of 0.013 %/cycle (0.33 %/day, Cl−) and 0.024 %/cycle (0.60 %/day, Br−). Electrochemical and spectroscopic experiments reveal that the high stability arises from selective reduction of [NiII(dppe)2X]+ vs NiII(dppe)X2 which allows for a more efficient ligand-coupled electron transfer (LCET) process in which halide dissociation is the only change to the coordination environment. We further show that addition of dppe during cycling experiments can halt capacity fade and even regenerate some lost capacity over time.

item.title: Scalable Alkylation-Cyclization Strategy for Bridgehead-Functionalized Fused Tetrahydrofurans
item.description: This study presents a practical and scalable synthetic platform for the preparation of functionalized fused tetrahydrofuran building blocks, addressing a current gap in the accessible chemical space. The methodology is based on an alkylation/cyclization sequence of readily available cyclic β-ketoesters with 1,2-dibromoethane under mild K2CO3/18-crown-6 conditions. The transformation proceeds in a single operational step, avoids hazardous reagents, and was demonstrated on a multigram scale. The protocol accommodates five-, six-, and sevenmembered carbocyclic systems as well as selected heterocyclic substrates, providing the corresponding bicyclic tetrahydrofuran derivatives in high yields. The resulting scaffolds bear synthetically versatile vinyl ether and ester functionalities, enabling straightforward diversification through electrophilic addition, catalytic hydrogenation, and ester-based interconversions.

item.title: Site-Selected Oxygen K-Edge X-ray Circular Dichroism in Methyl Lactate−Water: Electronic-State Character, Intermolecular Proximity, and Spectral Cancellation
item.description: Hydrogen bonding can place an achiral molecular fragment in a chiral environment, yet the electronic character and methodological robustness of its site-selected X-ray circular-dichroism response remain challenging to establish. Here, we investigate oxygen K-edge excitations in a hydrogen-bonded methyl (S)-lactate−water complex using r2SCAN-3c geometries, siterestricted TDA-TDDFT, and natural transition orbital (NTO) analysis. Although the selected water-oxygen 1s orbital is strongly localized, the resulting excitations exhibit distinct waterlocal-like and solute-associated charge-transfer-like (CT-like) electron distributions. Introducing diffuse basis functions at the PBE0 level reverses the energetic ordering of these patterns and changes the signs of their character-matched rotational strengths. With a common ma-def2-TZVPP basis, PBE0, CAM-B3LYP, and ωB97X-D3 predict local−CT energy separations of 0.269, 1.447, and 1.522 eV, respectively. Across these common-basis calculations, the local-like state remains the lower excitation with negative velocity-form rotational strength, whereas the CT-like state remains the higher excitation with positive rotational strength. Despite these differences, PBE0 and CAM-B3LYP yield nearly identical integrated velocity-form spectral cancellation of approximately 46.5% at a Gaussian full width at half maximum of 0.6 eV within the integration window from E1 – 1.5 to E1 + 6.0 eV, compared with 54.9% for ωB97X-D3. However, this near agreement is sensitive to the integration boundaries and does not persist quantitatively across the tested windows. Thus, similar integrated attenuation can conceal substantially different electronic-state distributions. Fixed-geometry separation controls show low-energy excitation energies approaching isolated-water references and velocity-form rotational strengths becoming negligible at the reported numerical precision. Transition-moment analysis further identifies coordinate-origin dependence as the dominant source of anomalously large distant-pair length-form rotational strengths in the investigated calculations; analytical re-expression relative to the water oxygen substantially restores length−velocity consistency. Small rigid water displacements also modify the local−CT energy separation while preserving the dominant NTO localization patterns and the signs of the corresponding rotational strengths. Together, these findings establish an environment-sensitive theoretical water-site chiroptical response and demonstrate the importance of electronic-state character, coordinate-origin consistency, and spectral overlap for its interpretation. The conclusions apply to the selected fixed molecular configurations and do not constitute an experimentally calibrated or configurationally averaged XCD prediction.

item.title: GPU-Accelerated Evaluation of MP2 Correlation Energy Densities for Machine Learning of Density Functionals
item.description: Second-order Møller–Plesset (MP2) correlation energy densities can serve as ingredients for machine learning (ML) of density functionals that improve upon MP2-based double hybrids. However, limitations of existing implementations have restricted the evaluation of these energy densities and of ML-based functionals employing them to small systems. Here, we develop a GPU-accelerated implementation for evaluating MP2 correlation energy densities and their regularized and spin-resolved variants by combining a density fitting scheme that preserves high pointwise accuracy with memory-efficient tensor contractions. We demonstrate the use of the resulting energy densities in ML-based density functional approximations (DFAs) through the previously developed MLS2 model [Nat. Commun. 16, 11306 (2025)] and limMLS2, a variant introduced here that enforces a high density limit constraint to MLS2. The GPU-accelerated evaluation of MP2 energy densities enables routine application of these ML-based DFAs to systems described by more than 5000 atomic orbitals, with predictions remaining robust to the density fitting approximations and grid sizes tested. Overall, by making MP2 correlation energy densities accessible for larger systems, our work broadens their use in the development and application of highly accurate ML-based DFAs.

item.title: A Real-Space, Regularization-Invariant Metric for Density-Functional Error: A Proof of Concept on Fundamental Diatomics
item.description: Measuring the error of a density-functional approximation in space, rather than in energy, requires recovering the exchange–correlation potential from a correlated density, and we show that this ill-posed inversion governs the result: the magnitude of any metric defined directly on the potential varies by up to 12.8× across the usable window κ ∈ [10⁻⁷, 10⁻⁵] of the regularization parameter while the density it reproduces moves by at most 2.1×, and the position of its maximum is displaced by 0.31 Å when the one-particle basis is doubled, twice the physical scale the scan is meant to resolve. We introduce MAPA, which projects that error through the static Kohn–Sham linear response function, generalized to fractional occupations, so that what is measured is the electron density the error would displace: analytically gauge invariant, exactly removing the null space of the response function, and varying by ≤ 9.4% over thirty-six inversions where the potential metric moves by 1.2–12.8×, and by ≤ 6.5% under the change of basis. Applied to ten diatomics—203 geometries, of which a density-reproduction criterion evaluated independently of the metric admits 118—MAPA separates the pathologies at a matched fraction of each equilibrium bond length, the self-interaction signature of H₂⁺ still growing at 1.5 Rₑ where every static-correlation and polarization signature has begun to decay, and locates error cancellation in the integral of the dissociation curve rather than at its peak. Because the construction compares two multiplicative potentials, it applies directly to local-density and GGA functionals.MetricMetricMetricMetric

item.title: Cross-Scale Structural Evolution in 2D Silicon Nanosheet Anodes upon Electrochemical Cycling
item.description: Silicon is a high-capacity anode material for lithium-ion batteries, but the large volume change accompanying lithiation drives structural degradation across multiple length scales. Reducing silicon to a two-dimensional architecture has been explored as a strategy to accommodate lithiation-induced deformation yet whether morphological stability of individual silicon nanosheets translates into dimensional stability of the composite electrode remains unclear. Here, two-dimensional silicon nanosheets (2DSiNSs) are produced directly from commercial silicon micropowder by liquid-phase exfoliation in an IPA/water mixture (1:1 v/v) and integrated within a carbon nanotube (CNT) conductive network. The resulting 2DSiNSs, with an average thickness of 21 nm, retain crystalline silicon character without pronounced additional surface oxidation. Three cells cycled at 0.2C delivered 1932 and 1625 mAh g⁻¹ after 100 cycles and 1520 mAh g⁻¹ at the end of a 117-cycle test, with Coulombic efficiency close to 99% after the initial cycles; the cells differed appreciably in the rate of capacity fade. Differential-capacity analysis shows that the lithiation and delithiation peaks remain recognisable while their amplitudes decrease with capacity. Post-mortem analysis reveals a pronounced cross-scale contrast: cycled 2DSiNSs remain predominantly sheet-like without obvious severe fragmentation despite amorphisation, whereas cross-sectional FIB-SEM shows the local electrode thickness increasing from 3.24 to 13.96 μm after 117 cycles. This cross-scale contrast provides the central observation of the work: preservation of sheet-like morphology does not ensure dimensional stability of the composite electrode.

item.title: Impact of 2,2’-Substitution on the Pi-Conjugation and Electronic and Optical Properties of Biphenyl-Based Molecules
item.description: Developing strategies to tune excitons or generate Wannier excitons in organic small molecules (OSMs) is an important area of research for advancing photoinduced processes in these materials. Density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations were carried out to investigate intermonomer conjugation in six functionalized benzene monomers and their corresponding six functionalized bisphenol dimers. The study considered two electron-donating substituents (–NH2 and –OCH3) and four electron-withdrawing substituents (–Cl, –Br, –CN, and –NO2). Calculations were performed at the B3LYP/6-31+G(d,p) level in toluene. The effects of functionalization on the dihedral angles, electronic structures, and optical properties of the monomers and dimers were examined through analyses of the HOMO and LUMO energies and UV–Vis absorption spectra. The DFT results reveal that 2,2′-functionalization of dimers featuring a bridging motif between the two benzene rings can give rise to coherently degenerate electronic states, particularly in the Cl-, Br-, and NO2-functionalized biphenyl systems. As such, the best strategy to generate coherent degeneracy in a dimer bonded between two benzene rings are 2,2’-functionalization with the functional groups of Cl, Br, and NO2.

item.title: Normalized Nucleic Acid Payload in Lipid Nanoparticles: A Perspective on the Harmonization of Published Data
item.description: Precise and consistent reporting of the nucleic acid payload per lipid nanoparticle (LNP) is important for advancing the understanding and development of nanomedicines. However, the reported number of RNA molecules ranges between ∼1-300 in recent investigations. To evaluate the RNA payload across investigations, we introduce and apply a normalized nucleic acid payload metric which accounts for differences in LNP size, nucleotides per RNA and N/P charge ratio. The normalized payload results in a similar value for siRNA-and mRNA-containing LNPs of different LNP sizes, where the average value of 73±17 nucleotides/zeptoliter agrees well with the expected payload density based on molecular packing arguments. The use of normalized payload harmonizes the reported payload, complements existing payload metrics and enables comparison across samples and measurement techniques at both the single-particle and ensemble-average level.

item.title: WISP: Learning Spin-Resolved Electron Localization from Atomic Environments
item.description: The electron localization function (ELF) has been used to identify bonds, lone pairs, and interstitial electrides, in materials ranging from thermoelectrics, batteries, and superhydrides. We train WISP to predict the spin-resolved electron localization function (ELF) from the atomic geometry and signed site moments of a periodic crystal. One network predicts both spin channels at any point in the crystal, using opposite signs of the moments. To improve accuracy in layered and porous materials, a far-field branch includes information from atoms beyond the local cutoff. A separate network predicts the moments when only geometry is available. The per-channel mean absolute error is 0.0106 on the zero to one ELF scale. Errors in the individual channels and their difference are smaller than for a two-head control with the same inputs. The predicted fields reproduce the spin contrast of MnPd and the interstitial maximum in the electride Sc₅Cl₈ without occupied orbitals as inputs, suggesting potential use in screening electrides and magnetic materials.

item.title: Protocol and Sampling Sensitivity of Residue Rankings from MM/PBSA and MM/GBSA Decomposition
item.description: Residue-level molecular mechanics/Poisson–Boltzmann surface area (MM/PBSA) and molecular mechanics/generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA) decomposition is often used to select residues for mutagenesis or design. Rankings depend on the endpoint protocol, sampled trajectory and residue set. Using DecompStat, we compared matched-frame energy differences, signed rank correlations and top-k overlap for polycystin-1 (PC1)/p17, diclofenac–cyclooxygenase-2, insulin–insulin receptor (IR) and BRAF(V600E)–LY3009120. In the historical, unreweighted mixed-contact PC1/p17 run, correlations between generalized Born (GB) and Poisson–Boltzmann (PB) profiles over 870 entities were 0.217–0.325, although 16–17 top-20 residues were shared. In three selected 5-ns insulin–IR trajectories from two preparation clusters, median Spearman correlations across 975 residues were 0.855 between trajectories at fixed protocol and 0.336 between protocols within trajectories. On one common 54-residue set (1.0 kcal mol⁻¹ cutoff), these medians became 0.807 and 0.877, while top-20 Jaccard medians remained 0.667 and 0.818. For BRAF, new endpoint analyses of 300 frames from each of three published 5-µs runs gave correlations of 0.244–0.303 for GB5 versus GB8 at fixed mbondi2 radii, despite 18–20 shared top-20 residues. Changing radii within GB8 gave 0.990–0.997. Correlated synthetic controls showed undercoverage of the original nominal 95% moving-block bootstrap intervals; residue differences are therefore reported as observed magnitudes. We recommend reporting the residue set, protocol and top-k overlap alongside rank correlations. The comparisons assess numerical rankings, not the physical accuracy of endpoint models or mutation effects.

item.title: AnCore: A Six-Stage Structure-Based Virtual Screening Pipeline Integrating Two-Phase Redocking, Reciprocal Rank Fusion Consensus Scoring, and a Contact-Anchored Elastic-Network Pose-Persistence Heuristic
item.description: Structure-based virtual screening workflows often keep molecular visualization apart from multi-engine consensus rescoring and post-docking triage. We present AnCore Scientific Studio (v1.2.0), an open-source macOS workbench that couples a Rust/Tauri shell and a 3Dmol.js viewport to a six-stage Python pipeline. The stages are (1) receptor curation with AMBER14/GBn2 minimization and a steric clash gate; (2) a two-phase co-crystal redocking gate, with local BFGS refinement (Phase A) and focused-box Monte Carlo search (Phase B); (3) RDKit ligand preparation; (4) consensus rescoring of AutoDock Vina, Vinardo and AutoDock4 by Reciprocal Rank Fusion and mean Z-score; (5) 3D radial interaction fingerprinting; and (6) post-docking triage, made up of unrestrained full-atom minimization (Mode A), a 3.0 ps contact-anchored elastic-network pose-persistence heuristic (Mode B) and export of 100-ns explicit-solvent OpenMM/GROMACS packages (Mode C). We tested the pipeline on a five-target development benchmark (1IEP, 3ERT, 1UYG, 1M17, 1STP; 50 ligands, 25 literature actives and 25 presumed-inactive decoys, plus 5 co-crystal references). All five co-crystal ligands passed the 2.00 Å redocking gate (mean RMSD 0.906 ± 0.388 Å). Consensus rescoring raised the suite-mean ROC-AUC from 0.584 for Vina alone to 0.696 for mean Z-score (one-sided paired bootstrap p = 0.0070). A contact-count control that uses no co-crystal information reached 0.864, and the Mode B heuristic reached 0.920. Because the Mode B parameters were set during development on these same targets, and because its inputs overlap with the contact counts it is compared against, we treat these two figures as in-sample results. Mode B also rejected 40% of the actives under hard cutoffs, so it should be used for ranking and not for rejection. Prospective validation on independent DUD-E and LIT-PCBA targets is still needed.

item.title: Sunlight-Driven Photo-Reductive Mineralisation of PFOS under Ambient Conditions
item.description: Perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are highly persistent molecules whose widespread use and global distribution have created an urgent need to develop effective remediation strategies. Here, we address this research gap by exploiting zinc sulfide (ZnS) for the photo-reductive mineralisation of PFASs under natural sunlight and ambient conditions. We found sulfur vacancies (Vs) within the ZnS lattice, produced during supercritical synthesis, to be responsible for visible-light absorption and enhanced photocatalytic activity. Complete mineralisation of PFOS was achieved in both batch (3 mL) and continuous circulating flow (12 mL) after 24 h of ultra-violet (UV-A, 365 nm) irradiation. Analysis of transformation products and scavenger studies revealed that C–F bond cleavage was driven by direct photoelectron reduction. The treatment of various PFASs and field-derived aqueous film- forming foam (AFFF) contaminated water revealed chain length and head group dependent activity associated with compound adsorption and reduction potential (from density functional theory calculations). Ultimately, the demonstrated natural sunlight activity (under ambient temperature and pressure) highlights the potential of supercritical ZnS as a scalable, sunlight-active PFAS remediation technology.

item.title: Probing Metal-Organic Framework Stoichiometry Using Quantitative NMR and TGA
item.description: Metal-organic frameworks do not always have perfect stoichiometry because of defects, modulators, or mixed linkers. A common approach to quantify these defects is to define a value for ‘missing linkers’, typically by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). In this approach, the researcher must isolate the mass loss attributable to the linker and make a priori assumptions about the material composition. To eliminate this potential source of error, we propose using the (metal oxide) residue from TGA to quantify metal content, combined with quantitative NMR spectroscopy of a digested sample to quantify the linker content. We demonstrate this approach for three examples: MAF-6, ZIF-8, and MOF-5.

item.title: Oxidation and temperature limits of sharp ZrB2–SiC nose tips in hypersonic flight: a coupled screening model
item.description: Sharp-edge flight envelopes consider temperature alone, yet sharp ZrB2–SiC nose tips can also fail by losing their protective borosilicate glass or by SiC active oxidation. We couple stagnation-point heating, conduction and a layered oxidation model to map the Mach numbers and altitudes at which a tip lasts 30 minutes. Four mechanistic findings come from comparing runs of the same model, so they depend less on its absolute accuracy than the maps do. First, conduction into the flank is the largest single physical effect, placing the 30-minute boundary of a two-dimensional nose-tip model 0.5–2.75 Mach above that of one-dimensional stagnation-line maps, conditional on the flank heating. Second, the glass evaporation coefficient decides whether glass loss or the temperature limit ends the life but moves the boundary by at most 0.5 Mach. Third, with a passive-to-active line fitted to pooled data, SiC active oxidation is never the first failure at flight oxygen pressures of 2–220 kPa, though low-pressure ground tests can show it. Fourth, the heating, glass emissivity and silica balance control the time to failure in two base cases. The model fails every furnace, arc-jet and plasmatron validation check. Its fully catalytic surface is hotter than every measured one, which is on the safe side, but its glass lasts longer than in the plasmatron. Its absolute 30-minute boundaries are thus screening estimates not shown to be conservative. Because the failure mode depends on oxygen pressure, ground tests need to reproduce flight pressure and gas composition as well as heat flux.

item.title: Enabling rational design in flow organolithium chemistry through data-driven guidelines for substrate selection, reaction choice, and electrophile compatibility
item.description: A practical setup for continuous-flow organolithium chemistry is presented, based on >1000 substrate-electrophile combinations across aromatic, heteroaromatic, and aliphatic scaffolds, including “enabling” building blocks. Despite flow lithiation's recognized advantages in heat transfer and reproducibility, systematic criteria for predicting which transformations translate well to continuous operation, and which should remain batch, have been lacking. By mapping solubility constraints, thermal stability limits, and competing pathways in this substrate set, we elaborated decision rules that allow chemists to assess flow compatibility before committing resources, select appropriate bases and temperature windows, and anticipate common failure modes. Validated through multi-hundred-gram to kilogram syntheses with productivities up to 1 kg h-1, our protocols address a gap between laboratory demonstrations and process implementation, providing an empirically grounded tool for adopting flow organolithium chemistry in practice.

item.title: Donor and Acceptor Branching Suppresses Hydrogen-Bond Cooperativity in Mixed (NH3)m(H2S)n Clusters
item.description: Ammonia and hydrogen sulfide are both weak hydrogen-bond (HB) donors, yet each molecule can donate and accept more than one HB, so their mixed networks branch readily. We use the molecular tailoring approach (MTA) at the MP2/aug-cc-pVTZ level to obtain the energy of every HB in 20 neutral (NH3)m(H2S)n clusters (m+ n = 3–7) and to split each energy into an isolated-dimer term and a cooperative term. The acceptor atom sets the energy scale: HBs accepted by nitrogen average 3.98 kcal mol−1 and those accepted by sulfur 2.28 kcal mol−1, and the S–H· · ·N bond is the strongest contact in almost every cluster (up to 7.49 kcal mol−1). Cooperativity is modest, 0.68 kcal mol−1 per HB or 21.8% of the total HB energy, and a sizeable minority of HBs are anticooperative. It is ordered mainly by local branching. With a branching index κ defined as the number of extra HBs donated by the donor molecule plus the number of extra HBs accepted by the acceptor molecule, the mean cooperative energy falls from 1.32 kcal mol−1 at κ = 0 to 0.28 kcal mol−1 at κ = 2 (Spearman ρ = −0.74). The S–H· · ·N bond, the strongest in isolation, is also the most sensitive to branching. At the cluster level, the cooperative share of the total HB energy falls from 33% in a monocyclic tetramer to 11% in a fused, branched heptamer. Branching thus provides a simple predictor of where a mixed HB network gains or loses non-additive stabilisation, and it indicates which contacts pairwise or uniformly scaled many-body models are likely to misdescribe.

item.title: Synthesis and Reactivity of Spirocyclopropyl Amines: A New Class of Conformationally Constrained Building Blocks for Drug Discovery
item.description: Spirocyclopropyl amines combine the conformational constraint of a spiro center with the electronic character of the cyclopropane ring, yet saturated azaspirocycles bearing two such rings remain scarce. Herein, we report the synthesis of mono- and dispiro-cyclopropyl saturated N-heterocycles from readily available lactams and cyclic imides via the Kulinkovich-de Meijere reaction and its Bertus-Szymoniak modification. The approach covers pyrrolidine, piperidine, piperazine, morpholine, thiomorpholine, thiomorpholine 1,1-dioxide, azepane, and 1,4-diazepane cores, and provides the first examples of dispiro-cyclopropyl piperidines, piperazines, morpholines, and thiomorpholines. Key intermediates were obtained in up to 95 g per run. Reductive Ndebenzylation with H2 over Pd/C in the presence of HCl is complete in 2 h and gives the parent amines in over 85% yield. Each spirocyclopropane lowers the pKa of the ring nitrogen by 0.7-1.5 units and raises logD by 0.4-0.5 units, which is 0.1-0.3 units less than the corresponding gem-dimethyl group. In human liver microsomes, tetramethyl substitution accelerates clearance up to 30-fold, whereas the dispiro benzamides are more stable than both their monospiro and their α-unsubstituted analogues.

item.title: Grain Boundary and Stress Evolution during Thin Film Growth: Key Factors Governing the Resistive Hydrogen-Sensing Characteristics of Palladium Thin Films
item.description: Palladium thin film resistive hydrogen sensors have attracted considerable attention due to their high selectivity and low-temperature operation, yet the microstructural mechanisms governing their sensing performance remain insufficiently understood. Here, we establish a processingstructure-property framework by integrating controlled Pd film growth, sensing-performance evaluation, multiscale structural characterization, electron-transport modeling, and DFT calculations. Film thickness and deposition temperature were systematically varied to tune grain growth in Zone Ⅱ Pd films, enabling the structure-performance relationships to be mapped. The resulting trends showed that increasing film thickness suppressed baseline drift but reduced sensitivity and response rate, whereas higher deposition temperatures shifted the critical thickness for drift elimination to smaller values. To uncover the structural origin of these trends, a Mayadas-Shatzkes-based transport model was developed to quantify the contribution of grain-boundary scattering. The model identifies grain-boundary density as the dominant microstructural factor governing sensitivity in the films, with its reliability further supported by independent validation using datasets obtained at deposition temperatures not included in model calibration. Characterization across different film thicknesses further reveals an evolution from defect-rich non-twin boundaries toward more stable boundary configurations, which is considered to suppress irreversible hydrogen retention and improve baseline stability. Residual strain from thermal mismatch and intrinsic stress evolution may influence hydrogen incorporation and sensor sensitivity, partly explaining deviations from the grain-boundary-based model. These findings establish a mechanistic framework linking film growth, microstructural evolution, and sensing performance, providing a practical basis for structure-guided optimization of Pd thin film hydrogen sensors.

item.title: Biorelevant Triplet μ1,2-Peroxodicopper(II) Intermediates in a Bis(tridentate) Dinucleating Ligand Framework
item.description: Type III dicopper proteins function as O2 carriers and catalysts for hydroxylation reactions, and our understanding of relevant Cu2/O2 intermediates has benefited greatly from studying synthetic analogues. The O2 binding mode in synthetic peroxo intermediates is strongly dependent on ligand effects, including the denticity of the ligand. Here we report a first example of a μ1,2-peroxodicopper(II) complex with bioinspired {N3} coordination that emulates the proposed initial stages of O2 binding in dicopper proteins. The pyrazolato-bridged bis(β-diketiminato) ligand (L3−) forms complexes [LCu2]− (1−) and [KLCu2] (1K) that feature “T-shaped” copper(I) ions and a nearby K+ in 1K. They smoothly react with O2 even in the solid state to give [LCu2(μ1,2-O2)]− (isolated as [K(Cryptand)]2) and [KLCu2(μ1,2-O2)] (2K), which have been fully characterized, including by X-ray diffraction, rRaman and UV−vis spectroscopies, complemented by DFT calculations. SQUID magnetometry reveals ferromagnetic coupling with unusually large zero-field splitting, and spin Hamiltonian parameters have been quantitatively analyzed by frequency-domain THz-EPR. Complex 2−, with a Cu–O–O–Cu torsion angle close to 90° and an S =1 ground state, represents a rare ⊥P type peroxo complex. Comparison with the few other μ1,2-peroxodicopper(II) complexes, whose structural and magnetic properties have been experimentally established, reveals magnetostructural correlations. 2− shows very high affinity towards K+ ion to form 2K (Ka in the range of 105−107 M−1 in THF), which enhances stability and leads to different thermal decay pathways. Preliminary reactivity studies of 2− indicate unusual hydrogen-atom abstraction from TEMPOH to form 1− as well as oxygen-atom transfer to reactive phosphines. This work expands the structural and electronic/magnetic landscape of Cu2/O2 intermediates and provides key mechanistic insights into O2 activation at dicopper sites.

item.title: A stopping rule for completing computed phase diagrams with generative models
item.description: Phase diagrams constructed using known phases misjudge stability when key phases are missing. Generative models supply as many structures as needed, but how many structures to generate and which diagrams will change are unknown. We add 10,000 MatterGen structures per system, relaxed with a machine learning interatomic potential, to Materials Project (MP) data for six Li–transition-metal–O ternaries and track the hull convergence. The responses fall into two groups: Li–Ru–O, Li–Hf–O, and Li–Zr–O (70–107 MP structures) gain 4–9 stable candidates and exhibit total convex-hull shifts of 59.9–62.9 meV/atom, whereas Li–Mn–O, Li–Co–O, and Li–Ni–O (240–609) exhibit a minimal hull shift. When reduced to 70 MP structures, the latter gain a similar number of stable candidates by rediscovering removed hull phases. The hulls converge within 5,000–8,000 structures. After generating 8,000 structures, a stopping rule, tested using Li–Ir–O, decides whether more are needed. Density functional theory places seven Li–Ru–O compositions 5–83 meV/atom below the MP-only hull but rejects the potential’s false positives in well-explored systems. This gives a stopping rule and early diagnostic for incomplete phase diagrams.

item.title: Reaction-Dependent Predictability of Yields from Small Substrate-Scope Datasets
item.description: We evaluate structure-based regression using molecular fingerprints and ElasticNet across four reaction datasets (96–190 reactions). The models outperform constant-yield baselines for two transformations, including literature-assembled umpolung amide synthesis. Learning curves reveal reaction-dependent data requirements, with useful predictions emerging from 20 training examples in favorable cases.

item.title: Frustrated Lewis Pairs upon UV light absorption: ground vs excited state mechanisms in CO2 adduct formation.
item.description: The broadly reported increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration is a major contributor to global climate change. In response, substantial efforts are being directed toward the development of low-carbon energy systems and the identification of efficient CO₂ capture technologies to mitigate the excessive greenhouse gas emissions. Among these, solid sorbent-based capture methods have attracted significant attention.[1] However, a key limitation of such approaches lies in the regeneration of the sorbent material, which often requires energy-intensive processes.[1,2] To address this challenge, systems capable of reversible CO₂ capture triggered by a nondestructive external stimulus—such as light—offer an appealing alternative. Such systems could enable tunable CO₂ uptake and release, facilitating not only dynamic capture but also the transport and controlled release of CO₂ in line with conventional Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) strategies.

item.title: The photoelectric effect as frequency coupling: a spectral law without work function, photons, electrons or energy
Minimalist catalyst for excellent tacticity: Stereocontrolled radical polymerization with Lewis acids
item.description: Stereoregular vinyl polymers are made by coordination or anionic polymerization, whereas radical polymerization, the dominant industrial route, offers little stereocontrol. We report a simple Lewis acid–mediated reversible addition–fragmentation chaintransfer polymerization: with only 3.3 mol% samarium Lewis acid, polymerization of more than a dozen functionalized acrylamides reaches up to 97% m diad selectivity, the highest tacticity in homogeneous radical polymerization of a commodity monomer. A single samarium center coordinates the radical chain end and the incoming monomer, fixing its addition orientation. The isotactic polymer resists backbone degradation in acid and base, and in hydrogels, isotactic and atactic chains reinforce the networks differently. This method provides a minimalist route to diversify polymer properties from one monomer feedstock and offers a new strategy for stereocontrolled radical polymerization.

item.title: Mesoporous Separator Engineering Rectified Electrolyte Chemistry for Durable Non-Aqueous Aluminium-Ion Batteries
item.description: Rechargeable non-aqueous aluminium-ion batteries (AIBs) are promising low-cost and sustainable energy storage systems, but their development is hindered by sluggish transport of strongly associated chloroaluminate ions and unstable aluminium plating/stripping. Here we demonstrate that engineering the separator microenvironment effectively regulates electrolyte chemistry and interfacial ion transport in AIBs. A binder-free dendritic mesoporous silicamodified glass fiber (DMS-GF) separator is developed by growing DMS nanoparticles directly 2 at the GF scaffold surface. The resulting silanol-rich mesoporous architecture weakens anioncation interactions in chloroaluminate electrolytes, promotes ion dissociation, and shifts electrolyte speciation towards the electrochemically active Al2Cl7 - species, leading to enhanced ionic mobility. The interconnected mesoporous channels further homogenise ion transport and electrolyte distribution, enabling highly reversible and stable aluminium plating/stripping with suppressed dendrite growth. In graphene//Al full batteries, the DMS-GF separator enables high reversible capacity, improved rate capability, and long-term cycling stability, outperforming pristine GF separators. This work demonstrates that separator microenvironment engineering can synchronously regulate electrolyte chemistry and interfacial electrochemical processes for high-performance AIBs, providing a promising strategy for controlling ion transport in unconventional battery systems.

item.title: Orbital-Optimized Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Within the Tamm-Dancoff Approximation Using Lagrangian Minimization
item.description: Time-dependent density functional theory in the Tamm-Dancoff approximation (TDDFT/TDA) is a computationally tractable approach for calculating excited electronic state energies and properties. TDDFT/TDA constructs single-excitation electronic states from Kohn-Sham molecular orbitals where the occupied orbitals have been variationally optimized according to the Aufbau principle and the virtual orbitals are left unrelaxed. To investigate the effects of incorporating state-specific orbital relaxation into the single-excitation determinant, a Lagrangian-based state-specific orbital-optimization (OO) method is derived where stationarity of a targeted TDDFT/TDA Lagrangian with respect to orbital rotations is enforced using the analytic orbital-rotation gradient. Rigorous test calculations on vertical excitation energies across valence, Rydberg, fluorescence, and charge-transfer (CT) excitations spanning configuration interaction singles (CIS), global hybrid, and range-separated hybrid functionals reveal distinct functional-and state-specific trends. Specifically, OO-CIS improves 75.6% of singlet valence excitations relative to conventional CIS. For CT excitations, the range-separated hybrid rCAM-B3LYP yields a significant improvement, reducing the mean absolute error by 0.233 eV, whereas other global and range-separated hybrid functionals show less improvement or worse performance. Furthermore, for some transitions orbital optimization can significantly underestimate excitation energies, revealing critical challenges when relaxing orbitals in the TDDFT/TDA framework.

item.title: End-to-End Learning from Experimental Data: Integrating the PC-SAFT Equation of State into Neural Network Training for Improved Polymer Parameter Estimation
item.description: Accurate and computationally efficient thermodynamic models are essential for the design, optimization, and operation of many (bio)chemical processes involving polymer solutions, blends, and membranes. In this work, we combine machine learning (ML) with the PC-SAFT equation of state (EoS) to predict the non-associating pure component parameters for polymers, enabling the rapid evaluation of the pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) behavior of polymer melts and rubbers. Using a dataset of more than 5,400 PVT measurements for 78 chemically diverse polymers, we systematically evaluate the effects of EoS integration in the training process, the molecular representation, neural network architecture, and transfer learning. A baseline approach trained on pre-fitted PC-SAFT parameters is compared with a physics-informed approach that embeds the EoS in the training loop, enabling end-to-end training directly on experimental PVT data. Performance is assessed using 6-fold cross-validation. For a feed-forward neural network (FNN) using extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs), embedding the EoS reduces the average mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 8.67% to 5.57%. Replacing the FNN and ECFP representation with a graph neural network (GNN) using cyclic polymer graphs further reduces the average MAPE to 2.58%. Pre-training the models on PC-SAFT parameters for small molecules, followed by fine-tuning on polymer PVT data, yields additional improvements, reducing the average MAPE to 5.06% for the FNN and 2.15% for the GNN. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining an embedded EoS with geometric deep learning and transfer learning for accurate polymer PVT predictions.

item.title: nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT: Spin-complete mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT with a noncollinear exchange–correlation kernel
item.description: We present nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT, a spin-complete mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT with a complete noncollinear exchange–correlation response. The theory unifies the two extensions of MRSF-TDDFT, the noncollinear kernel of nc-MRSF and the spin-complete closed–virtual (CV) space of CV-MRSF, in a single response operator. Three parameter-free rules supply every density-functional interaction that the completed CV space requires: the transverse kernel is added wherever exact exchange acts, the Coulomb interaction of a singlet-coupled CV pair is completed with its longitudinal kernel, and the semilocal spin potential enters one-electron elements as its spin average. As a result, the response yields spin-pure states, is covariant under separate closed, singly occupied, and virtual orbital rotations, and recovers the isolated Tamm–Dancoff excitation matrices of a closed-shell fragment separated from the reference open shells, which triplet-pair degeneracy alone does not ensure. With 20–25% exact exchange, nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT gives lower Thiel singlet and triplet errors than either parent method. At this common optimum of nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT and conventional TDDFT for singlet excitations, the singlet excitation energies of the two methods are comparable, while the B1LYP singlet–triplet gap MAEs on Thiel and QUEST are 71–77% lower with nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT than with conventional TDDFT in the RPA or TDA. However, the principal advantage of the method lies beyond vertical excitations: as a spin-complete mixed-reference response that treats ground and excited states on an equal footing, it is expected to carry this accuracy into strongly correlated regimes where single-reference TDDFT fails, including diradicals, bond breaking, doubly excited states, and conical intersections.

item.title: How Chemical Evidence Shapes Mechanistic Reasoning and Prediction by Large Language Models: Fine-Grained Inference in Nucleoside-Derived Supramolecular Gelation
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) offer a distinctive capability for chemical problem solving by integrating chemical knowledge and experimental evidence through reasoning expressed in natural language. Yet how chemical evidence reshapes their predictions and expressed rationales is not self-evident and has received limited examination, particularly for challenging chemical problems. Here, using nucleoside-derived supramolecular gelation as a testbed, we systematically varied the evidence provided to LLMs and quantitatively evaluated their predictions and the mechanistic alignment of generated rationales. Without additional evidence, correct predictions were associated with greater alignment to literature-supported mechanisms than incorrect ones, suggesting that LLMs can draw on intrinsic chemical knowledge despite rationales remain largely general. Structurally similar gelation precedents, thought improved prediction accuracy significantly, reduced this distinction by anchoring rationales to insufficiently discriminative structural features, indicating that similarity-based evidence does not necessarily improve chemical reasoning and that prediction accuracy alone is insufficient to assess LLM performance in chemical tasks. In contrast, condition-constrained references and mechanistic information more consistently directed rationales toward chemically discriminative features, even when prediction accuracy did not improve in tandem. Together, our study highlights the importance of task-specific evidence design and quantitative rationale evaluation for reliable chemical problem solving by LLMs.

item.title: The Multi-Objective Computational Design and Prioritization of Novel TSPO PET Radioligands for Improved Inflammation Imaging after Traumatic Brain Injury
item.description: Clinicians employ TSPO PET imaging to quantify the extent of TBI-associated neuroinflammation through radioligands that bind to the central pocket of the human translocator protein. However, many radioligands underperform due to pocket dissociation and low blood-brain barrier permeability. I hypothesize that a targeted cheminformatic pipeline can accelerate the pre-synthetic design of novel TSPO ligands with improved physicochemistry. Eight second-generation ligands were benchmarked using preclinical physicochemical and PET metrics. Emapunil was selected as the modifiable scaffold. Haloalkylation was curated across two functional groups, establishing a 1922-analog dataset. Following prioritization based on molecular descriptors and docking energy, 15 lead candidates (assigned IDs of A#) proceeded to PBPK modeling. Leads were z-scored, and the top three candidates advanced to plasma-input Logan analysis. Consensus ADMET prioritized leads for short-timescale molecular dynamics. The top four analogs were evaluated through a five-replicate 10-ns MD panel along with the reference, and retrosynthetic routes were devised through ASKCOS. A7 showed a significantly improved static and dynamic profile over emapunil. A7 displayed a 5.4-fold increase in partition coefficient and fourfold increase in brain-plasma concentration ratio in the PBPK simulations versus the reference. Logan VT slope estimates were stable for A3, A6, and A7. MD showed A7 retained 28.25±5.94 mean fixed-pocket contacts and ≥10 contacts in 97.96±2.04% of frames. A7’s contact advantage over AC-5216 was statistically significant after Holm correction (p=0.0317). ASKCOS predicted 200 complete synthetic routes for A3, A8, A15, and emapunil with buyable terminals, while A7 displayed an unresolved N-difluoromethylation terminal. Pareto analysis identified A7 as the only nondominated analog. A7 emerged as the strongest radioligand candidate and demonstrates the effectiveness of a cohesive cheminformatic system in PET radioligand development.

item.title: IRexp: A database of experimental infrared band lists from open-access literature
item.description: Machine-learning models for infrared (IR) spectroscopy are often trained on computed spectra, yet simulated spectra differ from measured ones, and large, open experimental IR datasets remain scarce. Here, we introduce IRexp, an open collection of 230,946 experimental IR band lists (cm⁻¹ peak positions) extracted from 19,859 open-access articles published between 2005 and 2026 and their supporting information, together with an author-entered Chemotion repository deposit. In total, 96,973 records are linked to a resolved structure, and 50,682 of these also carry author-reported ¹H and ¹³C NMR. Record quality was checked manually against the source documents and by automated consistency tests. IRexp holds more than four times as many experimental IR records as existing public IR spectral libraries, and every record keeps its source identifier and licence, with records released in licence-specific files. We expect IRexp to accelerate data-driven IR spectral prediction, automated structure elucidation, and multimodal models trained on real experimental data.

item.title: Matched Metal–Organic Frameworks Reveal How Chemistry and Pore Structure Shape Gas Adsorption
item.description: Designing metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for adsorption requires distinguishing pore-chemistry associations from differences in architecture. An outcome-independent matched-comparison analysis of the ARC–MOF v7 simulation database pairs frameworks with identical topology and dimensionality and closely constrained values of seven pore descriptors. The resulting 13,072 chemistry-changing pairs are benchmarked against similarly matched pairs with unchanged represented chemistry labels. Across 18 gas–temperature–pressure states, linker-family changes exhibit the most consistent adsorption separation beyond this empirical background, whereas coordination-compatible metal substitutions show more context-dependent behavior. Residual-geometry adjustment attenuates the linker-associated contrast by approximately 36–40% under the primary linear specification and 20–27% under the tested additive nonlinear specifications, while retaining an overall positive linker-associated signal. These model-dependent estimates do not identify a causal contribution from pore geometry. Uptake differences frequently contract at higher loading and need not translate into favorable working capacity or selectivity. Structure-resolved comparisons and common-protocol RASPA simulations reveal strong, near-null, and electrostatically sensitive cases without constituting independent experimental validation. The analysis establishes structurally matched observational comparisons as a practical route to interpretable chemistry–structure–adsorption relationships and helps prioritize follow-up modeling and measurement.

item.title: Assessing the transfer-learning performance of foundation models for energetic materials property prediction under low-data conditions
item.description: This study evaluates the performance of off-the-shelf foundation model embeddings provided by CheMeleon, MolCLR, and MACE-OFF to predict energetic material properties from sparse datasets. Models were trained to predict crystal density, heat of formation and impact sensitivity from SMILES strings, with performance benchmarked against molecular representations provided by Morgan fingerprints and hand-crafted descriptors. Overall, the foundation model embeddings were found to be competitive with the hand-crafted descriptors, with MACE-OFF showing the strongest performance in numerical regression tasks. Heat of formation was found to be the most predictable property (R2 = 0.72), followed by crystal density (R2 = 0.54) and impact sensitivity (R2 = 0.47). Testing under more demanding cluster-based data splitting revealed that MACE-OFF retained the strongest performance across representations, suggesting that its learned embeddings generalise more effectively than hand-crafted descriptors to molecules that are more dissimilar to the training set distribution. Predictability for impact sensitivity improved noticeably when recast as a classification task, where CheMeleon emerged with comparable performance to the hand-crafted descriptors. These results show that while foundation model embeddings can provide useful low-input screening tools for energetic materials, they are not yet a competitive replacement for the bespoke models trained on larger datasets.

item.title: A Novel Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7// Li4Ti5O12 Dual-Ion High Power Battery
item.description: Concerns over lithium abundance and safety have driven the search for alternatives to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are promising owing to sodium’s abundance and low cost, but sluggish Na+ diffusion and limited rate capability hinder their practical use in high power batteries. Here we report a mixed (Li/Na)-ion battery as a low-cost, high-power alternative solution. We demonstrate a novel mixed-ion Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7(NFPP)//Li4Ti5O12(LTO) full cell operating in a lithium-based electrolyte with excellent performance. The cell delivers an average operating voltage of 1.9 V, an initial capacity of 109.6 mAh g-1 and 80% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 1C, along with exceptional rate performance maintaining discharge capacities of 87.3 and 73.5 mAh g-1 at 10C and 20C, respectively. The results show that both electrodes undergo reversible Li+/Na+ co-intercalation via the Fe2+/Fe3+ (NFPP) and Ti3+/Ti4+ (LTO) redox couples. The cathode incorporates Li, reaching Na2.64Li1.16Fe3(PO4)2P2O7 at initial full discharge, while Na uptake into LTO is lower (Na0.87Li6.12Ti5O12 at initial full charge), as revealed by In-situ X-ray diffraction, ICP-OES and XANES. The long-term cycling stability, and high-rate capability, demonstrate NFPP/LTO as a high power, long-life Na/Li mixed-ion battery and provides new insight into mixed-ion charge-storage mechanisms to direct future research in this area.

item.title: Resin 3D Printing with Dose-Controlled Solubility
item.description: Vat photopolymerization (VP) offers high resolution and throughput with low surface roughness, but requires support structures that limit printable geometries, generate non-recyclable waste, and must be removed manually. We introduce dose-controlled selective solubility vat photopolymerization (dSSVP), wherein a low 405 nm light dose forms linear acrylate chains, while high doses deplete a base quencher and initiate cationic epoxide polymerization to form a solvent-resistant crosslinked network. Raman spectroscopy and cure depth measurements quantify the cure kinetics and inhibition period before epoxide polymerization begins. After printing and heat treatment, low-dose regions dissolve rapidly in food-safe solvents, while high-dose regions resist dissolution and exhibit a bending modulus of ≈3 GPa. A variety of complex demonstration prints are presented, including a dental aligner, an MIT “Brass Rat” class ring, and an assembly of interlocked parts. Further advancement of dSSVP could enable fully automated production of finished parts using widely available single-resin desktop VP hardware.

item.title: Plasma-Enhanced Surface Doping SnNiOx Nanofilms for Water Oxidation
item.description: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) limits the efficiency of alkaline water electrolysis, and the rational design of non-precious-metal anodes requires an understanding of how a dopant modifies an oxide surface. Although atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) offer high intrinsic activity, precise synthesis and characterization of their local active sites remain challenging. Surface doping provides a tractable alternative for probing intrinsic activity and correlating it with the dopant coordination environment. Here we use plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PE-ALD) to deposit sub-monolayer doses of Fe and Co on ultrathin SnNiOx films grown on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO). We vary the Fe and Co dopant coordination environment using oxidizing (O2) or reducing (H2) plasma as an independent variable on the dopant deposition step.
