item.title: Modeling IR and VCD Spectra of L-Phenylalanine Polymorphs with Polarizable Force Field Molecular Dynamics
item.description: Building on the computational framework developed by Bowles et al. [J. Chem. Phys. 158, 094305 (2023)] for IR and VCD spectroscopy of alanine in the gas and condensed phases, we employ a polarizable AMOEBA-based approach to investigate solid-state vibrational spectra. We investigate the vibrational properties of two distinct L-phenylalanine (Phe, C9H11NO2) polymorphs: the anhydrous Powder form and the hemi-hydrated Fiber structure. Phenylalanine forms complex crystalline architectures stabilized by extended zwitterionic (−COO− · · ·−NH+ 3 ) hydrogen-bonding networks, whose influence on vibrational properties remains challenging to characterize. We demonstrate that polarizable molecular dynamics simulations provide an effective approach for reproducing the solid-state IR and VCD spectra of these polymorphs. While the IR spectra exhibit largely similar features, the VCD spectra show pronounced differences between the Powder and Fiber forms, providing a sensitive spectroscopic fingerprint of their distinct supramolecular arrangements. These results highlight the enhanced sensitivity of VCD to intermolecular effects and crystal organization and establish polarizable molecular dynamics as a promising approach for characterizing structural polymorphism in molecular crystals.

item.title: Electrochemistry in air enabled by electric-field spillover at three-phase interfaces
item.description: Electric-field spillover at dielectric/electrolyte/electrode interfaces drives electrochemical reactions in traditionally forbidden environments, including insulating liquids and gases. Here, we show that ferrocene present in either air or toluene undergoes concerted electron- and phase-transfer at the molecularly thin 3-phase boundary, resulting in its oxidation and the transfer of the reaction product, ferrocenium, into the aqueous phase. A detailed investigation of the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of these reactions reveals that concerted electron- and phase-transfer in air proceeds substantially faster than in the liquid dielectric, toluene. These remarkable differences are the result of smaller solvation constraints, shorter electron-tunneling distance, stronger electronic coupling, and faster diffusion of reactants. Our findings establish electrochemistry in air as a platform for rapid interfacial reactions.

item.title: RGST-ΔSCF: Response-Guided Construction and Tracking of Excitation-energy-Resolved states along surface Reaction Pathways
item.description: Illumination can promote or inhibit catalytic reactions, yet the origin of their excitation-energy dependence remains unclear. Here, constrained ΔSCF calculations and spin- and k-resolved wavefunction-overlap tracking are used to follow nonequilibrium electronic configurations across four excitation-energy intervals along H2-dissociation pathways at doped Cu/ZnO interfaces. The preferred pathway switches from final-state-referenced configurations at low excitation energies to initial-state-referenced configurations at higher energies, with dopant-dependent crossover energies and nonmonotonic barrier responses. Metal-site dopants regulate reactivity primarily through excitation-induced reconstruction of collective metal-H bonding, whereas support-site dopants act through pathway-dependent interfacial spin redistribution. Neither excitation energy nor the magnitude of charge, bonding, or spin redistribution alone universally predicts catalytic promotion; the response depends on its direction, localization, and differential coupling to the initial and transition states. Application to Ag-mediated O2 dissociation further demonstrates that population-dependent interfacial reorganization, rather than net adsorbate charge alone, controls bond activation.

item.title: Sulfur Nitrosylation by Cytochrome P460 Can Complete the Catabolic Primary Metabolism of Ammonia Oxidizing Bacteria
item.description: Ammonia oxidizing bacteria (AOB) generate reducing equivalents for cellular respiration via the multi-electron oxidation of ammonia (NH3) to nitrite (NO2–). Two steps are known: the hydroxylation of NH3 to hydroxylamine (NH2OH) by ammonia monooxygenase, and the oxidation of hydroxylamine NH2OH to nitric oxide (NO) via hydroxylamine oxidoreductase. However, the details of the process by which NO is oxidized by one electron to NO2– remain unknown. Herein we discuss a possible source of this final electron via the nitrosylation of low molecular weight thiols (RSHs) by the conserved AOB protein cytochrome (cyt) P460. The resulting S-nitrosothiols (RSNOs) bear nitrogen in the same oxidation state as NO2–, and have been shown to yield NO2– upon hydrolysis. We show that low molecular weight RSHs are abundant in the periplasm of the AOB Nitrosomonas europaea, where principal ammonia catabolizing enzymes are localized. We demonstrate that cyt P460 is competent for S-nitrosylation via an electrophilic {FeNO}6 intermediate, and that electron transfer attends this process in the presence of an electron acceptor. Reaction rates for reactions of the emergent FeII form of cyt P460 are quantified and shown to be slow relative to oxidation by an electron acceptor. We also establish that this reactivity is operative in cyt P460 variants that, despite proteomic abundance, are incompetent for NH2OH oxidation. Together, these results implicate cyt P460 as the next and presumably final enzyme used by AOB for ammonia catabolism after HAO.

item.title: Martini on Autopilot: A Modular Toolset for Expert- and Agent- Driven Parameterization
item.description: Coarse-grained models such as Martini 3 enable simulations of large systems over extended timescales, but extending the force field to new molecules remains challenging due to the manual, expertise-driven nature of parameterization. Existing tools focus on mapping or bonded parameter assignment, yet are often limited in scope, lack accuracy for more demanding applications, and provide little support for validation or systematic molecular construction. Here, we present a modular toolset for the parameterization, fragment-based assembly, and validation of molecules in Martini 3. The approach integrates tools for assisted mapping (CGbuilder), parameterization and bonded validation (shaker), evaluation of partitioning behavior (taster), and programmatic assembly of molecular fragments (mixer). Rather than bypassing the iterative nature of parameterization, these tools provide a structured framework for constructing, evaluating, and refining coarse-grained models while remaining interoperable with existing Martini workflows. We demonstrate the approach through the fragment-based parameterization and assembly of a series of PROTACs, showing that independently validated warhead, recruiter, and linker fragments can be combined to reproduce atomistic reference properties and experimentally observed trends in lipophilicity and membrane permeability. Finally, we show that the same infrastructure can support autonomous parameterization by an LLM agent, which independently derived bonded models with accuracy comparable to expert-guided parameterization and substantially exceeding that of the fully automated approaches evaluated here. Together, these results establish a common infrastructure for structured, quantitative, and iterative Martini parameterization that can support expert developers, autonomous agents, or combinations of both.

item.title: Redox Activation and Electric-Field Control of Spin Localization in a Diamagnetic Hexavanadate
item.description: Electrical control of molecular spins typically exploits pre-existing paramagnetic centers. Employing a synthetically widely used redox-active Lindqvist-type hexavanadate as a model platform, we combine density functional theory (DFT) with spin dynamics simulations of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to establish the relationship between molecular charging, spin localization, and magnetic response. A transverse electric field of 0.3084 V·Å–1 reverses the energetic preference between competing spin-localization configurations of the two-electron-reduced cluster in both vacuum and acetonitrile solution. The four-electron-reduced cluster favors an antiferromagnetically coupled singlet (S = 0), while alternative singlet localization patterns approach energetic degeneracy under the applied field. Although the isotropic g factors vary comparatively modestly, electric-field-dependent anisotropic g and 51V hyperfine tensors yield distinct magnetic resonance signatures. Spin dynamics simulations predict field-sensitive hyperfine features at X band for the one-electron-reduced cluster and pronounced direction-dependent W-band responses for selected paramagnetic configurations of the four-electron-reduced cluster. Finally, long-lived reduced hexavanadate clusters on a graphene sheet are not accessible under equilibrium conditions because the electron transferred from the POM relaxes back into the conducting support through the strong image-charge interaction.

item.title: Stackable Force Fields in GROMACS: Addons and Mixed 1–4 Scaling
item.description: Hybrid biomolecular simulations routinely combine building blocks described by different force fields, yet the GROMACS topology format and its preprocessing tools have long assumed a single, monolithic force field whose 1–4 electrostatic and Lennard-Jones scaling factors are global to the whole system. We introduce force field addons: self-contained .ffa directories that contribute atom types, bonded parameters, and residue, hydrogen, and terminus databases to a base force field at gmx pdb2gmx run time, with explicit compatibility declarations, priority-based resolution of overlapping definitions, and conflict detection. Native mixed 1–4 scaling complements them: the new [ addon_scaling ] and [ pair_scaling ] directives attach scaling factors to atom-type groups and to the torsion parameter records that prescribe the 1–4 interactions, with explicit wildcard-patterned overrides resolved by declared priority and silent inconsistencies turned into fatal preprocessing errors. With case-sensitive residue databases and automated AMBER-to-GROMACS conversion, GLYCAM-based glycans become usable alongside amber19sb proteins as first-class force field components; resolved topologies and per-term energies cross-check exactly against Amber references.

item.title: Translational Potential of New Academic Synthetic Transformations: Lessons from the Aza Paternò–Büchi Reaction
item.description: Despite steady advances in synthetic methodology, the reactions routinely used in medicinal chemistry have changed little over several decades, which suggests that discovering a reaction and establishing it as a practical tool are separate challenges. Academic methods are typically judged by yield, selectivity, and scope, whereas industrial adoption also depends on supply-chain security, reagent availability, and scalability. As a supplier of building blocks for drug discovery, we at Enamine examined this gap through a collaboration with the Schindler laboratory, aimed at translating the group’s 2019 visiblelight-mediated intramolecular aza Paternò–Büchi reaction into a commercial azetidine building block pipeline. Using an inexpensive organic photosensitizer, we successfully scaled the key [2+2] photocycloaddition in batch and flow, delivering 12 unique azetidine building blocks on up to 50 g scale, and accessed five additional scaffolds through post-synthetic modification. The remaining barriers arose outside the key step and traced to the oxime auxiliary that the cycloaddition requires, which limited both substrate preparation and access to free N–H azetidines. The findings from this case study show that translational readiness depends on the full synthetic sequence, and a stage-by-stage assessment identifies where further development is needed before industry uptake can be successful.

item.title: Chemoselective Suzuki–Miyaura Cross-Coupling of NHC–Aryl Boranes in the Presence of Boronic Esters: Sequential One-Pot Synthesis of Unsymmetrical Terphenyls from Aryl-Linked Diboron Compounds
item.description: N-Heterocyclic carbene (NHC)–aryl boranes (Ar–BH2–NHC) were found to undergo direct Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling (SMC) with aryl bromides under Pd2(dba)3/XPhos catalysis, with no activation step. The reaction tolerated a range of aryl bromides, including one bearing a C–Cl bond that was left untouched. In intermolecular competition with an aryl pinacol boronate (ArBpin), the use of K2CO3 as a base in toluene–H2O delivered the NHC–borane-derived biaryl with 99:1 chemoselectivity. Extension to aryl-linked diboron compounds bearing both NHC–BH2 and boronic ester moieties revealed that selectivity depends strongly on the diol ligand: the Bpin derivative showed poor chemoselectivity and often gave the double-coupling product, whereas the sterically hindered B(Epin) (Epin = 1,1,2,2-tetraethylethylene glycolato) derivative reacted with 99:1 selectivity at the NHC–borane site. Sequential addition of a second aryl bromide, K3PO4, water, and toluene to the same vessel enabled the one-pot synthesis of an unsymmetrical terphenyl in good yield.

item.title: OlefinCat-LLM: Full-Text Extraction and Chemistry-Guarded Ranking of Single-Site Polyolefin Catalyst–Process Packages
item.description: An industrial polyolefin grade, whether an EPDM tire compound or a solution-process polyolefin elastomer, is specified by melt index or Mooney viscosity, but it is made by a precatalyst package (metal center, ligand family, and activator role) and by a polymerization window of temperature T , pressure P , and Al/M ratio. Those fields sit in the nested experimental tables of papers and patents. An abstract usually names only a catalyst class and a product, so a grade request cannot be turned into a rankable catalyst–process row from the abstract alone, and recombining common literature labels creates activation packages that were never reported together. OlefinCat-LLM turns nested tables into reviewable metal–ligand–activator–process records. Experimental reports are collected by automated screening, the tables are expanded from the full text, and each shell is ranked only after a chemistry guard and a process window anchored on a reported experiment. The guard is required because a metalligand similarity cannot see the activator: V/VOCl3 keeps a cosine of 0.934 with documented alkylaluminum chlorides and with blocked MAO or borate. On an EPDM tire request the guard contracts 2160 proposed shells to 216 documented packages. The top-ranked shell on that request is a late-metal ethylene package. Inverse ranking on this platform supplies only a reference for reviewing packages against the industrial request.

item.title: Unveiling the Molecular Basis of Silver(I) Sequestration by Glutathione: Stoichiometry, Stability and Structure at Neutral pH
item.description: The complexation of Ag(I) ions by reduced glutathione (GSH) at neutral pH was studied by UV-vis, CD and NMR spectroscopies and mass spectrometry, aided by DFT calculations. A tetrameric Ag4(GSH)4 complex was found to be the sole species at these conditions, containing the octagonal Ag4S4 ring with digonal S-Ag-S coordination mode. The pH-independent stability constant of this complex was determined by competitive titrations with excess of thiosulfate ions as KAg4(GSH)4 = 1.6 × 1067 M-7. Equilibrium calculations using this constant indicate that physiological millimolar GSH concentrations can sequester all substoichiometric Ag(I) ions, presumably preventing their toxicity towards cellular proteins. However, the ring structure of the complex is not compatible with the standard cellular heavy metal detoxication mechanism. These results provide a molecular basis for deciphering the role of glutathione in cellular silver toxicity and detoxication.

item.title: Distributed Assembly Theory: Distinguishing Biological Causal Depth from Information Entropy via Recursive Fragmentation
item.description: Identifying agnostic biosignatures—measurable structural properties distinguishing evolved biochemistry from abiotic matter—remains a central challenge in astrobiology and cheminformatics [1, 13, 14]. Assembly Theory (AT) addresses this boundary through the molecular Assembly Index (M_A), a measure of constructional complexity defined by the minimal number of recursive bond-joining operations required to build a molecular graph while reusing previously assembled substructures [1, 15]. However, two major criticisms challenge this framework. First, critiques grounded in Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT) and Algorithmic Information Dynamics (AID) contend that M_A offers no fundamental advance over one-dimensional lossless compression, arguing that molecular assembly reduces to standard Lempel–Ziv dictionary proxies (zlib/DEFLATE and LZW) [4, 5, 7]. Second, computational critiques argue that exact M_A enumeration is intractable for complex natural products due to combinatorial subgraph explosion [1, 8].Here, we resolve this methodological impasse. We demonstrate that while canonical branch-and-bound subgraph isomorphism logic [8] is mathematically sound, legacy internal parallelization layouts (specifically untied #pragma omp task directives using shallow firstprivate object copies) exhibit a 100% segmentation-fault crash rate on cyclic macromolecules due to race-condition double-free heap corruption. To eliminate this concurrency bottleneck, we introduce an asynchronous, process-isolated orchestration architecture paired with standardized MDL V2000 graph serialization that enforces strict single-threaded execution within individual C++ traversals while expanding compile-time bitset tracking bounds to 4,096 bits. High-throughput scaling is recovered via external operating-system process isolation (ProcessPoolExecutor) across a 256 GB unified-memory compute architecture.Using this decoupled pipeline, we evaluated 397 benchmark molecules across four structural complexity classes—achieving 396 exact integer resolutions (99.75%, with 1 combinatorial-horizon timeout at 1,200 s and zero mathematical bound violations) and resolving the diterpenoid Paclitaxel (Taxol) in isolation to M_A=23. For each resolved structure, we compared exact M_A against 1D dictionary compressibility quantified via zlib/DEFLATE compressed SMILES byte cost per non-hydrogen heavy atom (C_"LZW" =L_"zlib" ("SMILES" )/N_"heavy" ) through the Causal-to-Compression Ratio (R_"MA/LZW" =M_A/C_"LZW" ) [7, 12]. Whereas 1D byte cost per heavy atom inverts physical complexity due to syntactic character redundancy—scoring simple abiotic solvents higher than complex natural products (mean C_"LZW" =2.773 vs. 1.835" bytes/heavy atom" , with "C" _20 "-" "C" _40 branched alkanes lowest at 1.573)—both exact M_A and R_"MA/LZW" exhibit strictly monotonic divergence across complexity tiers. Mean R_"MA/LZW" climbs sequentially from abiotic solvents (2.656, mean M_A=4.83) and primary metabolites (3.926, mean M_A=7.90) through stochastic "C" _20 "-" "C" _40 branched alkanes (5.704, capped at a hard abiotic ceiling of M_A≤11) to complex natural products (7.214, mean M_A=12.48, benchmark maximum R_"MA/LZW" =16.580), reaching 15.333 (M_A=23 at C_"LZW" =1.50" bytes/heavy atom" ) for Paclitaxel. These results demonstrate that evolved biochemistry combines high 3D constructional depth with modular substructure reuse—a dual topological signature that 1D string compression fails to resolve.Note on Version History: This manuscript is a comprehensive revision of our preliminary preprint, "Distributed Assembly Theory: Distinguishing Biological Causal Depth from Information Entropy via Recursive Fragmentation" (ChemRxiv, June 2026) [9]. The preliminary version utilized a heuristic BRICS retrosynthetic fragmentation approximation [3], which violated exact ⌈log_2⁡E ⌉ graph lower bounds on fused polycyclic macromolecules. This V2 manuscript supersedes the preliminary report by implementing exact C++ branch-and-bound graph enumeration [8], resolving OpenMP heap-corruption vulnerabilities, and establishing exact M_A/C_"LZW" divergence baselines.

item.title: Non-proteinogenic γ-aminobutyric acid reorganises L-arginine and L-lysine adsorption on Ca-montmorillonite through selective displacement and Ca2+ bridging
item.description: Prebiotic polymerisation in dilute aqueous solution is frustrated by hydrolysis, and mineral surfaces are a widely invoked route by which this bottleneck may have been overcome on early Earth and Mars. Smectite clays are strong candidates, because their permanent layer charge allows their hydrated basal surfaces to concentrate, orient and protect organic molecules. Natural organic inventories are mixtures rich in non-proteinogenic amino acids, yet adsorption on clays has been studied almost entirely one compound at a time. Here we use molecular dynamics simulations to resolve how γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a common meteoritic non-proteinogenic amino acid, modifies the adsorption of L-arginine and L-lysine on Ca-montmorillonite (STx-1b), with every surface contact resolved by functional group. GABA lowers the surface-associated fraction of L-arginine from 67% to 47% and of L-lysine from 58% to 51%. The loss is selective rather than proportional. Ammonium contacts are removed first, while the guanidinium anchor of L-arginine is retained and Ca2+-bridged carboxylate contacts carry a larger share of the surface contact of L-lysine. GABA associates with the surface mainly through Ca2+ bridges and forms Ca-nucleated multimers, whose partitioning between surface and solution depends on the co-adsorbing amino acid. The interfacial composition of an amino acid mixture therefore cannot be predicted from single-component behaviour. Clay-bearing rocks, including those targeted on Mars, may record a subset of the organic inventory filtered by competition and cation bridging, rather than the inventory itself.

item.title: Improving Structure Prediction for Intrinsically Disordered Proteins: High-Throughput Ensemble Generation via Torsion-Space Sampling and OpenMM Vacuum Relaxation
item.description: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) challenge traditional structural biology paradigms due to their lack of a unique tertiary structure. Structure prediction tools, including AlphaFold, frequently fail when applied to IDPs, artificially collapsing dynamic ensembles into static, over-compacted, or incorrect structures. Here, we present an improved, streamlined pipeline tailored for generating valid, highly variable starting conformational ensembles for high-throughput molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by integrating and optimizing existing sampling techniques. To assess the validity of this framework, we focus on the 95amino acid core region of the TAU8 isoform (TAU-F). The pipeline builds upon established random-coil polymer mechanics to sample biophysically allowed Ramachandran 𝜙/𝜓 torsion angle spaces using idealized peptide bond topology, bypassing traditional Cartesian-space self-avoiding walk bottlenecks. To eliminate downstream packing failures without the file-system overhead of traditional setups, steric overlaps are resolved on-the-fly by streaming backbone templates directly into an in-memory vacuum minimization engine powered by OpenMM. Applying this integrated workflow, a relatively small 100-model ensemble was generated with a 100% downstream convergence rate and zero structural clashes. To maximize computing efficiency, systems were solvated and simulated using Hydrogen Mass Repartitioning (HMR) within GROMACS, enabling an accelerated 4-fs time-step while maintaining rigorous thermal and potential energy stability at 300 K on a 40-core dual-NUMA architecture. This integrated pipeline provides a robust framework for high-throughput IDP structural research.

item.title: The Validation Split Defines the Discovery Claim in AI-Guided MOF Screening
item.description: Machine learning is becoming a gatekeeper for metal–organic framework (MOF) discovery, but its credibility depends on whether validation matches the chemistry of deployment. Here, we show that the train/test split is not a technical choice, but the statement of what a model can legitimately support. In a controlled, database-scale adsorption benchmark, we hold targets, descriptors, models, hyperparameters, and metrics fixed while comparing random, geometry-, metal-cluster-, functional-group-, linker-, and topology-held-out splits for CO2 and CH4 uptake. Random, geometry-, functional-group-, and linker-held-out evaluations support broadly similar conclusions, whereas metal-cluster and especially topology holdouts reveal much harsher transfer regimes. For CO2 uptake at 0.15 bar, random-forest performance drops from R2 = 0.758 under random splitting to 0.267 under topology grouping, and top-5% recovery falls from 62.2% to 37.6%. We introduce split-aware, structurally auditable validation as a foundation for trustworthy AI-guided porous-material discovery. Significance statement. High-throughput MOF screening increasingly uses machine learning to decide which candidates should be simulated, synthesized, or inspected experimentally. This paper shows that such decisions cannot be judged by random-split accuracy alone. The same data, descriptors, models, and metrics can support a strong interpolation claim while weakening under a harder reticular-transfer claim. By treating the split as a chemistry-facing variable, we show that validation design changes not only regression scores, but also the identity of candidate shortlists. The resulting validation framework turns model evaluation into a traceable materials-screening argument: define the transfer problem, disclose elite-list survival, and route validation-fragile candidates to structural inspection, uncertainty analysis, additional simulation, or targeted data acquisition.

item.title: Sparse Hierarchy Integration-Inspired Protocol (SHIP): Hierarchical Exploration of Sparse-Reward Spaces with GFlowNets
item.description: Generative modelling is a useful methodology for large-scale combinatorial problems involving many possible candidates. Such problems typically suffer from exponential scaling in complexity as the size of the system being studied is increased, and this impedes search space exploration and discovery. This work explores the parallel between the problem of generating high-value samples from a high-dimensional distribution and choosing a sparse set of grid points for high-dimensional integration using the Smolyak hierarchy. The proposed method, called Sparse Hierarchy Integration-Inspired Protocol (SHIP), is a Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet) based framework in which high-value higher-dimensional samples are generated by extending up from high-value lower-dimensional samples sequentially and iteratively. This protocol is tested on a model problem of approximating path-integral solutions to open quantum dynamics using Small Matrix Path Integral for reward evaluation. We show that the capacity of this approach to circumvent problems related to poor reward connectivity is drastically improved when action space representation is updated based on interpretable features identified in solutions at intermediate steps. These results serve to motivate the implementation of this protocol more broadly for other generative problems in physical and chemical systems.

item.title: AutoSPS-D2B: Automated Solid-Phase Synthesis Expands the Reaction Scope for Direct-to-Biology Libraries
item.description: Direct-to-biology (D2B) has emerged as a powerful accelerant in early drug discovery, bypassing compound purification to compress the design-make-test-analyse (DMTA) cycle. However, the chemistry underpinning D2B libraries is limited to just a few sequential transformations using assay-compatible reagents and solvents. By contrast, solid-phase synthesis (SPS) empowers a far broader range of reactions and is highly amenable to multistep synthesis, yet its potential as a source for D2B libraries remains largely underexplored. In this study, we develop AutoSPS-D2B, a fully automated solid-phase synthesis workflow that converts multistep, resin-bound chemistry into crude screening libraries that can be assayed directly, expanding reaction scope well beyond the reach of solution-phase D2B. We applied AutoSPS-D2B to explore several distinct chemotypes as allosteric ligands for the immuno-oncology target CCR2. Good agreement was observed in the relative binding affinity trends between crude and pure screening compounds, enabling streamlined ranking of analogues and prioritisation of hits for further investigation. When applied to the advancement of a previously underexplored CCR2 hit, AutoSPS-D2B enabled an analogue space of more than 1,700 building block combinations to be rapidly sampled, leading to optimised compounds with up to six-fold binding affinity improvements in just two DMTA cycles. This work establishes automated SPS as a versatile and efficient engine for D2B-driven hit-to-lead discovery.

item.title: Flow-Through Capture Reversed-Phase to Hydrophilic Interaction Chromatography HRMS/MS to Expand Chemical Coverage in Environmental Non-Targeted Analysis.
item.description: Chemical coverage remains a major limitation in environmental non-targeted analysis (NTA), as conventional one-dimensional liquid chromatography (1D-LC) provides incomplete retention and separation across the broad physicochemical space of complex samples. To extend NTA coverage, we developed an online two-dimensional liquid chromatography–high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (2DLC–HRMS/MS) approach that combines reversed-phase (RPLC) and hydrophilic interaction (HILIC) selectivity modes. Flow-through capture (FTC) modulation collects the unretained RPLC fraction using a dual-trap system combining a porous graphitic carbon and a trimodal reversed-phase, cation- and anion-exchange sorbents, recovering complementary sample polarity space regions within a single analysis. FTC effective transfer to HILIC was tested on a LogD-representative set of six polar and mobile contaminants of emerging concern (CECs), with recoveries generally ranging from 35–100%. Feature detection assessment in water samples revealed a 2.3–2.6-fold increase in FTC 2DLC vs the individual HILIC and RPLC methods. By FTC 2DLC yielding a broader separation space, data-independent componentization demonstrated that precursor-associated MS/MS information increased and was successfully distributed across both HILIC and RPLC chromatographic domains. Fragment Ambiguity Score (FAS) analysis further confirmed low-ambiguity and structurally informative fragments within the expanded separation space. Our results show that exposing the flow-through fraction from RPLC separation to HILIC-MS expands the measurable chemical space and provides fragmentation information relevant to structural annotation, supporting FTC RPLC→HILIC–HRMS/MS as a promising strategy to increase chemical coverage in environmental NTA.

item.title: Activationless Charge Transport in Heliobacterial Reaction Centers: Polarizable Cofactors Coupled to Strong Intraprotein Electric Fields
item.description: We study rate-limiting steps of electron transfer following photoinduced charge separation to the primary acceptor A0 in a heliobacterial reaction center (HbRC). Two steps involved are electron transfer to the iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) FX of HbRC, followed by electron transfer to the FA ISC of a ferredoxin protein in solution. Ferredoxin forms a stable binding configuration with the reaction center as established by Brownian dynamics simulation. Molecular dynamics simulations are used to calculate the reaction times of ∼ 0.1µs (A0 → FX) and ∼ 3− 5µs (FX → FA). These two steps are the slowest in the overall electron transport in HbRC. Electron transfer to ferredoxin is irreversible since the calculated time of recombination to the closest A0 cofactor is ∼ 70 ms. All reactions show near-zero activation barriers when cofactors’ polarizabilities are included in the calculations. The overall robust operation of solar energy conversion in HbRCs is allowed by combining cofactors’ polarizabilities with strong local intraprotein electric fields.

item.title: The Distance to Gap Closure Sets the Triplet Energy of Phenylenes
item.description: The lowest triplet energy of a conjugated hydrocarbon is often estimated from its HOMO–LUMO gap. In phenylenes this estimate can be far off. Two isomers with nine benzene rings have the same Hückel gap, yet their triplet energies differ by 0.35 eV with Pariser–Parr–Pople electrons. The reason is that the triplet does not stay at the ground-state geometry but relaxes toward geometries at which the gap closes. We therefore characterize a carbon skeleton by its closure threshold ρ, the smallest relative change of the bond couplings that closes the Hückel gap. The threshold is fixed by the Kekulé structures of minority sign, so all phenylenes with the same sequence of linear and angular rings share it. In the Hückel–Su–Schrieffer–Heeger model the triplet energy is bounded by the energy needed to reach a geometry with a closed gap and stays close to a fixed fraction of it. For all 467 classes of tree-like phenylenes with up to nine rings, ρ ranks the triplet energies better than the gap at the ground-state geometry, with and without electron interaction, and density-functional calculations on all 170 classes with six to eight rings confirm the ranking. The distance to gap closure thus orders the triplet energies of a whole family from the carbon skeleton alone.

item.title: Graph-Theoretical Analysis of Electrochemical Swelling in Conducting Polymers
item.description: Understanding how electrochemical swelling reorganizes the morphology of conducting polymers is one of the central challenges in organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors because this process ultimately governs charge transport and device performance. Although molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed structural information, they do not directly quantify how swelling modifies the connectivity and topology of transport networks. Graph theory offers a natural framework for this purpose, yet a fundamental methodological question has remained unanswered: how should polymer morphology be represented as a graph so that graph-theoretical (GT) descriptors faithfully capture the underlying physics? Here, we address this question by performing a systematic GT analysis of an n-type conducting polymer poly(benzimidazobenzophenanthroline) (BBL) during electrochemical reduction. Physics-informed graphs are constructed from atomistic MD simulations at four levels of coarse-graining: atoms, aromatic rings, naphthalenic transport units (A-site), and entire polymer chains. The resulting graphs are analyzed using six representative GT metrics comprising three local (Average Degree, Degree Assortativity, Average Clustering Coefficient) and three global (Average Closeness Centrality, Average Betweenness Centrality, and Global Efficiency) descriptors. We show that electrochemical swelling transforms BBL from a compact transport network into a swollen porous heterogeneous gel with reduced long-range connectivity and increasingly important transport bottlenecks. More importantly, we demonstrate that the same GT metrics can describe fundamentally different structural features depending on the level of coarse-graining. The atomistic, ring, and A-site representations respectively probe swelling and pore formation, π–π contact organization, and mesoscale aromatic linkages. These findings establish graph theory as a powerful complement to conventional MD analysis and provide a general methodological framework for interpreting transport-relevant morphology in conducting polymers and other disordered soft materials.

item.title: Fourier Transform Method for Buried Surface Area
item.description: We develop a method that uses the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to efficiently calculate changes in the solvent accessible surface area (SASA) at many relative translations of two binding partners. For each binding partner, the buried surface area (BSA) is computed using the cross-correlation of a grid-based discretization of its SASA and of a solvent exclusion grid from its binding partner. This approach improves the tractability of exhaustive interface burial calculations by reducing computational complexity, making it particularly valuable for analyzing large biomolecular systems. We implemented an optimized library for Shrake-Rupley SASA by modifying sasa.cpp from MDTraj. Our approach reduces the cost of evaluating BSA at all translations within a rotation from to . One FFT pass costs 0.41–0.68 µs per translation against 0.14–1.70 s per pose for the direct calculation, a speedup of to that appears to grow with system size. Agreement with the direct calculation is close, with a root mean square error of 3.0 Å at 0.5 Å grid resolution. Possible applications of the method include virtual screening, models of biomacromolecular assemblies and aggregates, studies of protein diffusion, and thermodynamic analysis of large conformational ensembles.

item.title: Dual-Modality Attomolar Detection of DNA Hybridization Using Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity
item.description: Spin-selective charge transfer through DNA has emerged as a promising approach for DNA hybridization detection. However, the minimum DNA concentration at which a reliable spin-dependent signal can be experimentally observed remains unclear. Here, by employing the CISS effect, we report a dual-modality electrical and optical approach for detecting DNA hybridization. In electrical detection, we used a customized two-probe printed circuit board, which transduces a molecular-scale spin-based signal into a measurable macroscopic electrical signal. Photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy was also used to detect DNA hybridization, and time-correlated single-photon counting independently corroborated PL results through lifetime decay measurements. By using electrical and PL spectroscopy, we experimentally detect DNA hybridization down to 10 attomolar, with high reproducibility and selectivity against fully non-complementary DNA. Our results establish dual-modality electrical and optical measurements for ultrasensitive DNA hybridization detection and provide an experimental platform for spinselective charge transport in DNA.

item.title: Understanding the Orchestrating Role of TLR2 in Differential Heterodimerization
item.description: Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) recognizes microbial lipopeptides through heterodimerization with TLR1 or TLR6, but how distinct ligand recognition is transmitted across the membrane to promote intracellular signaling remains poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, and free-energy calculations to characterize the TLR2-TLR1 and TLR2-TLR6 dimerization, and to provide the most comprehensive atomistic models to date of full-length TLR2-TLR1 and TLR2-TLR6 heterodimers bound to their agonist lipopeptides. We reveal a distinctive conformational plasticity of the juxtamembrane regions: TLR2 populates both straight and bent conformations, whereas TLR1 and TLR6 predominantly explore energetically similar bent states. This behavior, together with membrane-dependent transmembrane association, enables TLR2 to orchestrate the differential heterodimerization by adapting its intracellular organization to its partner. Despite their similar architectures, TLR2-TLR1 and TLR2-TLR6 display markedly different dynamics, with TLR2-TLR6 forming a more rigid and interconnected complex and TLR2-TLR1 exhibiting greater conformational flexibility. These results provide a mechanistic framework linking ligand recognition, membrane organization, and partner-dependent dynamics in TLR2 signaling.

item.title: Bipolar Faradaic Water Dissociation in Bipolar Membranes
item.description: Water dissociation (WD, H2O → H+ + OH−) in bipolar membrane (BPM) junctions enables pH-asymmetric electrochemical devices, but the microscopic role of conductive WD catalysts remains unresolved. Here we show that conductive catalyst layers can drive nominally non-faradaic water dissociation through two spatially separated bipolar faradaic reactions. In this mechanism, the alkaline-side interface of the WD catalyst layer is polarized cathodically and reduces water by interfacial proton-coupled electron transfer (I-PCET) to form adsorbed or absorbed H equivalents and OH−, whereas the acidic-side interface is polarized anodically and oxidizes the same H equivalents to H+. Internal electronic conduction and neutral H transport close the circuit without requiring hydrated ions to cross the catalyst. Dense Pd membranes provide an ion-blocking model bipolar faradaic membrane (BFM); Pd, Pd-Pt and Pd-PtRu thin metal leaves embedded in BPMs reveal sidespecific H-transport limits; and Pd, Pt and PtRu nanoparticle layers show chemical-state control and selfactivation consistent with the same mechanism. These results provide new insights for BPM water dissociation, provide routes to crossover-free, low-overpotential BPMs, and show that even the simplest reaction of water can have multiscale transport phenomena governing its rate. One-sentence summary Conductive BPM catalyst layers can dissociate water through spatially separated faradaic reactions coupled by internal electron transport and neutral hydrogen-species transport.

item.title: Computational Drug Discovery of Natural Product Compounds for Tyrosinase Inhibition
item.description: Plants produce chemically diverse compounds for defence and survival, many of which exhibit biological activity and offer promising starting points for drug discovery. This study thus investigated natural compounds as potential inhibitors of tyrosinase, a key enzyme in melanin production and an established target in the treatment of hyperpigmentation. A quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) machine-learning model was developed using ChEMBL tyrosinase bioactivity data and property-matched decoys. Ten models, including decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting, were evaluated; logistic regression was selected for virtual screening. To make the model generalise to unseen chemistry, the model was tested on compounds that were required to have Tanimoto similarity of 0.40 or less to every training compound and to share no Bemis–Murcko scaffold with them. The model achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.78–0.86), compared with 0.56 using physicochemical properties alone. The frozen model was then used to screen 404,570 natural products from COCONUT (COlleCtion of Open Natural prodUcTs) and IMPPAT (Indian Medicinal Plants, Phytochemistry And Therapeutics). Of the top 1% of predictions, 1,694 compounds were both structurally novel and represented new scaffolds. Following computational filters for predicted skin permeability and potentially reactive chemical groups indicating skin irritation, the 100 highest-scoring candidates were selected for molecular docking. Docking reproduced the crystallographic tropolone binding pose with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.20 Å, while the most predictive docking score achieved an AUC of 0.64 (95% CI, 0.61–0.66). Among the ten highest-ranked candidates, two were associated with Anisomeles indica (Indian catmint) and two with Phaseolus lunatus (lima beans). These candidates warrant experimental validation and further investigation for potential dermatological applications.

item.title: History-Dependent and Irreversible Restructuring of Molecular Cu–N–C Catalysts
item.description: Copper–nitrogen–carbon (Cu–N–C) catalysts have been widely investigated for cathodic electrocatalysis, yet identifying Cu species under operating conditions and establishing structural reversibility remain challenging due to their dynamic restructuring. Here, we investigate the potential- and history-dependent evolution of a structurally well-defined Cu porphyrin model catalyst using cyclic voltammetry-coupled in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (CV-XAS), complemented by high-energy-resolution fluorescence-detected XAS, Raman spectroscopy, and identical-location electron microscopy. We show that cathodic polarization progressively generates metallic Cu species, with the extent of their formation depending on both the applied potential and prior electrochemical history. Changes in the XAS edge jump are consistent with potential-dependent Cu dissolution and redeposition, highlighting changes in apparent Cu inventory that are not captured by normalized XAS spectra alone. Importantly, although conventional XAS spectra recover features resembling those of the pristine Cu–N4 catalyst following open-circuit relaxation, complementary characterization reveals irreversible changes in the original molecular coordination environment and spatial distribution of Cu species under the investigated conditions. These findings distinguish the apparent recovery of conventional XAS signatures from irreversible molecular restructuring and highlight the coupled roles of electrochemical potential and polarization history in governing Cu–N–C catalyst evolution.

item.title: A vacated second ligand site acts as a decoy in redocking: systematic in P-glycoprotein, intermittent across eight other proteins
item.description: Redocking tests whether a docking protocol can recover a deposited pose: the ligand is removed and the program is asked to put it back. Standard preparation deletes every copy. When a structure contains two copies in one cavity, the receptor passed to the program was never observed empty. We measured the effect of that deletion in deposited human P-glycoprotein structures, with the search box centred on the deposited pose so that a failure cannot be blamed on site finding. Across 15 structures the median top-pose RMSD is 8.30 Å and 1 of 15 falls within 2.0 Å. Accuracy does not track the density support of the deposited ligand. That was the registered hypothesis, and it is not supported (Spearman ρ = −0.004, p = 0.9899). In the nine structures that carry a second copy, retaining the copy as rigid receptor moves the median from 8.26 to 3.46 Å and improves 8 of 9 (p = 0.0078). A carbon-only ghost of the same shape, which the scoring function sees as apolar volume but not as a hydrogen-bonding partner, agrees with the retained copy (p = 0.1289), while a box reduced to the same volume does not (p = 0.2969). The displaced poses lie in the vacated subsite (mean overlap 0.216 to 0.539, p = 0.0078). The comparison reproduces in rDock, which shares no code with smina: 6 of 7 structures improve, and the median falls from 8.35 to 3.67 Å (p = 0.0469). On eight unrelated proteins the same protocol does not support one direction (5 of 8, p = 0.3750), although trypsin moves from 8.59 to 0.50 Å. A scan of 37,596 PDB entries found 4,774 multi-copy sites across 929 proteins. A redocking number for a multi-copy structure should be reported both with the other copies removed and with them retained. Scientific Contribution. Published evidence for this preparation effect was one ligand in one structure. The comparison here covers nine two-copy P-glycoprotein structures, and a carbon ghost together with a volume-matched box separates apolar occlusion from polar ligand chemistry and from the volume searched. Repeated on eight other proteins, the same comparison does not support a consistent direction.

item.title: Effect of PDMS Sponge-Derived Silicon Oxycarbide Particles on Water Incorporation and Rheology in PDMS–THF Mixtures
item.description: Here we report preparing silicon oxycarbide (SiOC) particles from the commercially available polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), with radically different morphologies depending on the processing conditions. We first prepare PDMS sponge, which acts as the precursor material for the SiOC particles, by heating a solution of PDMS and cross-linker in THF with suitable concentrations. The cross-linking reaction simultaneously occurring with the bubble formation from boiling the THF results in the formation of a sponge. The sponge pieces are kept under two different thermal environments which yield silicon oxycarbide with entirely different morphologies. Sponges open to the atmosphere and subject to slow heating to 550 °C and slow cooling yield a soft powder, whereas covering it inside an aluminium foil and subjecting to fast heating and fast cooling yields a brittle solid film. XRD, FT-IR and XPS confirm SiOC formation. The SEM imaging of the soft powder shows particles of nearly spherical shape with sizes ranging from 100-500 nm whereas the brittle solid when crushed and ground, shows much larger particles. The BET surface area was found to be 4.36 m2∙g−1 and 190 m2∙g−1 respectively for the soft the brittle powders. These particles remarkably enhanced the miscibility of water in the binary mixture of PDMS-THF, with a concurrent enhancement in viscosity as water was added. Adding 1.25 wt% of soft and brittle particles to a 5:4 mixture of PDMS-THF increased its viscosity by 1.5 and 2 times respectively and could accommodate up to 40 wt% water without phase separation. Addition of 30 wt% DI water to the PDMS-THF-particle mixtures led to an increase in viscosity by nearly ten-fold and twenty-fold respectively with soft and brittle particles. Viscosity enhancement upon the addition of water can be attributed to increased hydrogen bonding between the water molecules and particles and the enhanced surface of the particles.

item.title: Artemisitene converts cysteine to dehydroalanine via a cascade reaction involving: (i) thiol-Michael reaction, (ii) oxidation of the sulfur atom, and (iii) elimination
item.description: Artemisitene, which contains both an activated olefin and an endoperoxide, is a plant natural product isolated from the medicinal plant, Artemisia annua. Recent efforts in our research laboratory have shown that a related sesquiterpenoid, arteannuin B, undergoes a thiol-Michael addition with cysteine. Therefore, we hypothesized that the presence of the α,β-unsaturated lactone in artemisitene, would also result in a nucleophilic addition of the thiol moiety of cysteine, and this adduct would also result in an oxidation to yield dehydroalanine. A time course experiment with artemisitene, N-acetylcysteine methyl ester, and triethylamine in deuterated dimethylsulfoxide revealed a reaction between artemisitene and N-acetylcysteine methyl ester, to ultimately form dehydroalanine over time. This study enhances our understanding of the medicinal properties of Artemisia annua, in particular, through the two functional groups present in artemisitene: an α,β-unsaturated lactone and an endoperoxide.

item.title: Metal-Free Spin Crossover Through Nitrogen-Intercalated Graphene Under Pressure
item.description: Spin crossover (SCO) phenomena, in which the spin state of an atom changes due to an external stimulus, have been the subject of ongoing research interest to this day. However, the considered atoms have been limited to transition metals like iron or cobalt. In this theoretical study, we show for the first time that external pressure can cause a nitrogen atom, i.e., a non-metal, to transit from a high spin (HS) to a low spin (LS) configuration. This nitrogen atom is located between two graphene sheets (N@Graphene) to mediate anisotropic pressure, serving as a proof-of-principle system on a periodic density functional theory (DFT) level. With increasing pressure, the distance between nitrogen and the graphene sheets decreases, leading to a SCO at a pressure below 5 GPa. To understand more about the mechanism behind the SCO, a finite model system, N@Circumcoronene, was constructed to allow the application of various electronic structure analysis tools for finite systems. These tools confirm that the SCO is the result of a closed-shell-dominated interaction in the sandwich structure. This work introduces a promising basis for the realization of a new class of materials with pressure-sensitive SCO involving main group atoms.

item.title: AutoSPS-D2B: Automated Solid-Phase Synthesis Expands the Reaction Scope for Direct-to-Biology Libraries
item.description: Direct-to-biology (D2B) has emerged as a powerful accelerant in early drug discovery, bypassing compound purification to compress the design-make-test-analyse (DMTA) cycle. However, the chemistry underpinning D2B libraries is limited to just a few sequential transformations using assay-compatible reagents and solvents. By contrast, solid-phase synthesis (SPS) empowers a far broader range of reactions and is highly amenable to multistep synthesis, yet its potential as a source for D2B libraries remains largely underexplored. In this study, we develop AutoSPS-D2B, a fully automated solid-phase synthesis workflow that converts multistep, resin-bound chemistry into crude screening libraries that can be assayed directly, expanding reaction scope well beyond the reach of solution-phase D2B. We applied AutoSPS-D2B to explore several distinct chemotypes as allosteric ligands for the immuno-oncology target CCR2. Good agreement was observed in the relative binding affinity trends between crude and pure screening compounds, enabling streamlined ranking of analogues and prioritisation of hits for further investigation. When applied to the advancement of a previously underexplored CCR2 hit, AutoSPS-D2B enabled an analogue space of more than 1,700 building block combinations to be rapidly sampled, leading to optimised compounds with up to six-fold binding affinity improvements in just two DMTA cycles. This work establishes automated SPS as a versatile and efficient engine for D2B-driven hit-to-lead discovery.

item.title: CIPER: Interpretable Permeability Predictions Guide Cyclic Peptide Editing
item.description: Each new analogue in a synthetic cyclic-peptide library requires synthesis and permeability measurement, making the choice of an edit consequential. Molecular difference learning predicts the effect of a modification; we ask whether explicit structural comparisons can also identify the measured analogues supporting its selection or parent retention. CIPER, short for Context-Integrated Potential Edit Regression, learns assay-matched permeability differences through a product of atomic and cyclic-residue kernels. Each prediction is an exact sum of signed training-molecule contributions. A comparison of 18 fixed-ranking and sampling methods covers 286 parent pools containing 4,213 measured candidate pairs. CIPER gives the highest one-query mean gain among the 13 methods sharing the permitted training labels under equal chemical-component weights. One CIPER query recovers 0.518 log10 units of improvement, exceeding 0.491 from four random queries; four queries reduce random-selection regret by 75.1%. Separate tests on 1,213 complete panels distinguish choosing an improving product from identifying parents worth retaining. Signed contributions expose supporting and opposing analogues in successful and missed recommendations, motivating synthesis tests across controlled changes in ring, tail and stereochemical context. CIPER makes the chemical evidence behind early candidate enrichment directly inspectable.

item.title: A mechanistic insight into the role of triplet states in excited-state deactivation of dibenzothiophene: a new fate for green chemistry
item.description: The environmental impact of petroleum derivatives is a current threat which needs to be studied and tackled in the present and near future. In this context, obtaining new insight about the degradation and remediation possibilities of polyaromatic sulphur heterocycles, and particularly dibenzothiophene, is a challenge requiring the full attention of the academic community. Thus, we have studied the dibenzothiophene excited state decay from a theoretical perspective, resorting to multiconfigurational methods, in order to obtain a full photophysical picture which until now was incomplete. Our results reveal the transitory generation of triplet species which supports the possible reactivity and desulphurization processes which were recently reported for this system.

item.title: synthmc: a precedent-based synthesizability score for transition metal complexes
item.description: Data-driven methods are increasingly being used for the in silico discovery of transition metal complexes (TMCs), ranging from machine learning models for high-throughput screening and generative models proposing new candidates to evolutionary algorithms for their de novo design. However, computationally discovered or designed TMCs are only rarely realized experimentally, in part because their synthesis is difficult and often not considered during the design process. At the same time, established synthetic accessibility scores for organic small molecules cannot be transferred to TMCs beyond their constituent ligands, as their fragment-based heuristics and molecular representations do not capture the influence of the metal center, coordination mode, and steric effects on coordinability. Here, we present synthmc, a precedent-based synthesizability score for TMCs that combines the precedent of ligands, coordination environments, and degrees of steric crowding in a reference corpus constructed from experimentally reported complexes in the Cambridge Structural Database. Evaluated on random and time-based validation sets, synthmc assigns, on average, lower scores to more recently reported complexes, consistent with their reduced precedent, indicating its ability to identify novel chemistry. We hope that synthmc will help to prioritize synthetically accessible candidates in high-throughput screening and generative design of TMCs and, more broadly, motivate the development of more comprehensive synthesizability assessments for TMCs, for example based on retrosynthetic approaches or expert evaluations.

item.title: The Same Edit, a Different Outcome: Relational Learning for Cyclic Peptide Permeability
item.description: The same local modification can enhance cyclic-peptide permeability in one chemical background and reduce it in another. Molecular difference learning predicts such changes from structure pairs, yet whole-molecule descriptors can merge stereochemically distinct edits. We test whether the residue relationships changed by an edit supply additional predictive information. Our edit-relational Gaussian process combines parent descriptors and their changes with signed counts of gained and lost residue relationships, preserving stereochemistry and ring, branch and tail connectivity. Across 286 parent pools and 4,213 measured pairs, the best measured improvement over the parent after two queries is 0.588 versus 0.54 log10 permeability units under equal component weights. Relational inputs improve this gain in all five evaluated chemical components under matched fitting and initial-mean ranking. Measured interaction panels contain 13 edit-preference reversals among 72 distinct-site comparisons, exposing the background dependence that the representation is designed to capture. Exact finite-pool analysis separates candidate resolution from measurement allocation. Controls sharing the first mean-ranked query locate the principal measured benefit in the representation and initial ranking. The findings motivate matched-edit experiments on new parents to test whether these relationships predict how permeability benefits transfer between backgrounds. An edited residue’s changing relationships provide a concrete, predictively useful description of its chemical context.
